Bank of Ireland notes that, as in this case, it could be decades before repayment fell due. Interest on your friend’s loan has been building up for 25 years.

Equity release borrowing by older homeowners jumps 30% to €75m

“To ensure customers would understand the product, the information provided clearly explained the terms of the loan,” a spokesman for Bank of Ireland says. And, having read the product brochure, those terms should be very clear to anyone who took the time to read it in full. It is not hidden in seven-point type.

“Most importantly,” the bank continues, “before any life loan was agreed it was a requirement for each customer to obtain independent legal advice – and to show that they had taken that legal advice – to ensure that customers fully understood the terms and conditions.”

Whatever about Bank of Ireland mis-selling this loan, there are questions about the advice any legal practitioner gave this woman back in 2003. She clearly did not “need” this money – or most of it anyway – as €100,000 has sat untouched on deposit ever since, effectively losing value. It is just such a bad call on so many levels.

So what “advice” the solicitor provided, I have no idea. I can see them saying they advised only on the legal and contractual issues rather than the wisdom of taking the loan but that seems a very narrow and unhelpful interpretation of their role.

Reader’s attempts to foil fraudsters hit weird Bank of Ireland roadblock

The bank certainly appears to be sticking to its view that the loan has worked exactly as it should and as it was advised to the client. It is simply unfortunate that it took so long for the details of this loan to emerge so that her extended family could help her.

]]>Gareth Fuller<![CDATA[How Irish businesses operating in both the North and South face ‘unnecessary’ barriers]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/27/businesses-that-export-cross-border-are-more-profitable-more-resilient/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/27/businesses-that-export-cross-border-are-more-profitable-more-resilient/Tue, 27 Oct 2026 06:00:00 +0000Crá, the successful Irish language TV detective series telling the story of a garda and a podcaster’s investigation into the discovery of a body in a bog in Donegal, tells us much about changing patterns in cross-Border trade.

]]>NurPhoto<![CDATA[Inheritance taxes: what your family needs to know about recent changes]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/27/inheritance-taxes-what-your-family-needs-to-know-about-recent-changes/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/27/inheritance-taxes-what-your-family-needs-to-know-about-recent-changes/Tue, 27 Oct 2026 05:59:00 +0000It may not have been much, but earlier this month, a number of changes were made to Ireland’s inheritance tax regime, which may ease the burden – somewhat – on families when they look to pass on the family home and other assets.

Indeed, an increase in the parent to child threshold means that a family with three children can now pass on an extra €60,000 tax free, or one with four children and 10 grandchildren could pass on an extra €120,000 tax free, thus saving the tax that would have otherwise arisen if the children had exceeded their thresholds.

So, what else might you need to know about changes to the inheritance, or capital acquisitions tax (CAT) regime?

Receipts on the rise

There is no doubt that the amount of CAT being collected by the Exchequer is on the rise, with the total yield surpassing €1 billion last year for the first time. This is more than double what was collected back in 2020. And inheritance tax is one of the main drivers of this, with some €968.4 million collected in 2025, up from €430.6 million in 2020, according to Revenue statistics.

More people are paying it, too. Figures show that 15,200 people paid the charge in 2025, up from 14,006 in 2024; 13,055 in 2023; and 11,376 in 2020. That’s a 25 per cent increase since 2020.

However, while there may be continued calls to increase the parent-to-child threshold further, the figures show that the biggest contributors to inheritance tax are those who leave money to relatives other than their children. The threshold for an aunt leaving money to a nephew or niece is quite low, at just €44,000. This means that a lot of the tax collected comes from this cohort – and it is on the rise.

As the table shows, so-called group B inheritances now account for 46 per cent of all receipts, compared with 41 per cent for parent-to-child transactions.

Did the changes go far enough?

The increase in the parent-to-child threshold of €20,000, or 5 per cent, will mean that someone inheriting €420,000 today, as opposed to before the budget, will save €6,600 in taxes. Group B, for transfers between relatives, also increased, from €40,000 to €44,000.

But is this enough?

Carl Donnelly is head of tax with accountancy and business advisory firm Cronin. He would have liked the Government to go further with the changes.

“It hasn’t really done enough in terms of where property prices are now,” he says, noting the continued increase in house prices. Today, for example, the median national price is €400,000 – or as much as €685,000 in Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown.

As Donnelly puts it, a child inheriting a three-bedroom house in Dublin, with a few thousand in savings, is going to “to end up a good bit over the threshold”, which will mean facing a tax bill.

He would like to see the parent-to-child exemption moved closer to €500,000 (this level was in fact last exceeded in 2009, when the threshold rose to €542,544), or for the introduction of some sort of exemption on the family home.

Biggest benefit

Those who stand to benefit the most from the latest changes are families who can avail of either CAT business relief or agricultural relief. This is because once certain conditions are met, these reliefs reduce the taxable value of the asset for gifts or inheritances by 90 per cent.

As Donnelly notes, if you have a parent passing on shares in a company or land that’s eligible for relief and is worth €4.2 million, its taxable relief will drop to €420,000 thanks to the relief.

“The €20,000 increase in the threshold actually allows for €200,000 worth of value to transfer tax free,” he says. “That’s kind of where the main benefit is. It can be quite useful”.

Home or savings

For typical families, however, the changes don’t amount to a lot.

“It’s better than nothing but it’s not a huge amount, and it’s not going to be life changing for families,” says Donnelly.

Alison McHugh, partner and head of private client tax services at EY, agrees that the increases were “relatively modest and are unlikely to fundamentally alter estate or succession planning strategies”.

However, she adds that they are nevertheless “a welcome development”, adding that they will at least help to mitigate the impact of asset price inflation, particularly in relation to family homes and business assets.

“For a family with four children and 10 grandchildren, this will allow an additional €120,000 of value to fall outside of the charge to Irish CAT,” she says.

There was increasing pressure before the budget to increase this by a substantial amount, given claims that the existing regime discriminated against single and childless people. However, the 10 per cent increase is unlikely to offer such relief.

“[The budget] hasn’t done anything for childless asset owners. A €4,000 increase is nothing in the grand scheme of things,” says Donnelly. Indeed, the increase means that someone would save €1,320 in tax thanks to the higher threshold.

As McHugh puts it, the change will help “somewhat”.

“For example, if you have no children but wish to split your estate between 10 nieces and nephews, this will allow you to give an additional €4,000 to each one, or €40,000 of value overall.”

One possible way to offer more relief is to allow a family home to be passed on tax free – no matter to whom it is transferred.

“It would alleviate a lot of concerns that childless homeowners have if the family home could pass tax free,” Donnelly says.

Consider a home worth €500,000 in Dublin. If this goes to a relative of the deceased, and they can use the group B threshold, then the inheritor will face tax at 33 per cent on €456,000 – or some €150,480.

“It can cause a bit of stress,” says Donnelly, noting that someone might inherit in August, and have to pay the bill by the middle of November − a short time frame in which to come up with such an amount, even if the intention is to sell the property.

Changing rates

An aspect of the recent budget that may have surprised was the decision to reduce capital gains tax to 31 per cent but to leave CAT at 33 per cent.

As Donnelly notes, if parents transfer a home to a child today, a CGT bill might arise on this transfer, while the child might face CAT, depending on their thresholds and the value of the property. This CGT can be used to offset the CAT charge but now they are being charged at different rates.

While “it’s probably rare that they’d equal each other,” Donnelly says, he adds that he’s surprised nonetheless that they don’t track each other.

“That’s something that might change next year,” he says, adding that, ideally, CAT would fall right back to 20 per cent, the rate it was at before the 2008 banking and property crash.

Small gifts

One area in which many would have liked to see change is the small gifts exemption. This has stayed at the €3,000 level for quite some time, and no change was made in the budget. It allows someone to receive a gift of €3,000, tax free, each year, from anyone. A couple could gift a child €6,000 each year between them (if they had it to give), or transfer up to €24,000 a year to a couple with two children.

“It would be great to see an increase in the small gift exemption as it has been €3,000 for a long time,” says McHugh. She adds that if this was increased to, say, €5,000, it could have a significant impact in allowing families to transfer wealth “in a more measured way but at a reduced tax cost”.

“It would also be helpful to families with no children as they could benefit a number of family members over a longer period of time at a significantly lower tax cost,” she says.

Donnelly agrees that the lack of a change was “very disappointing”.

“It’s a useful way for people to pass on bits of wealth,” he says.

So RTÉ is well used to unfavourable, and often unfair, comparisons. Unfair because the differences of scale are enormous, and with them come reservoirs of creative talent and technical resources that were always impossible to match on this side of the Irish Sea.

Still, having such a neighbour has generally been good news for anyone who cares about quality and editorial independence at RTÉ, because it offered a benchmark against which Montrose could be measured.

Less often compared is how the two countries’ political systems manage their relationship with public service broadcasting. That is even less flattering, and the same excuses do not apply.

The UK has far more rigorous and transparent structures for deciding what its national broadcaster is for and how to pay for it. Chief among them is the royal charter, renewed every decade after intense scrutiny and debate at Westminster. Ireland’s approach is ramshackle, as this month’s shambolic budget handling of RTÉ’s funding demonstrated.

Income from ‘broken’ television licence fee down €5.7m in first nine months

We are now on the cusp of an alignment as rare as a total solar eclipse. Both governments face the same deadline for deciding how to pay for public service broadcasting and make it fit for the mid-21st century. The BBC’s current charter expires on December 31st, 2027. So does the three-year funding deal struck for RTÉ in 2024.

In London, the process began last December with a green paper canvassing everything from modest licence fee reform to advertising and a premium subscription tier, followed by a public consultation and a lengthy House of Commons committee inquiry.

In Dublin, we had the Future of Media Commission, whose recommendation on funding was rejected. Whether that recommendation was wise is debatable, but it hardly justifies the procrastination that has followed.

In the UK, these questions are argued over in parliament, on a timetable fixed by the charter. In Ireland, they are settled, or not, in irate correspondence between departments, while a toothless Oireachtas committee goes in search of soundbites. Neither country faces an easy decision but, despite all its problems, the BBC is starting from a much better place.

One reason is that the UK licence fee rises with inflation under the current funding settlement and now stands at £180 (€212). The Irish fee, frozen at €160 for 18 years, would be about €195 had it kept pace with prices.

Last year, RTÉ received €183.5 million from the licence fee and €41.3 million directly from the exchequer. Indexation would have brought in roughly €40 million more, almost exactly the size of that top-up. Most of the so-called bailout was simply the cost of political reluctance to grasp that political nettle.

And that assumes the precipitous fall in licence sales still happened. There, too, the contrast is stark. Between 2022 and 2025, UK licences in force fell by about 4 per cent. In Ireland, sales fell by 19 per cent over the same period. Whether through evasion or households abandoning traditional TV, every lost licence hits the bottom line.

Only about four in 10 Irish households now buys a licence. Strip out those with no television, and the half a million or so with State-funded free licences, and somewhere between a quarter and two-fifths of those legally obliged to pay do not.

A household charge at the current rate, levied on everyone not entitled to a free licence, would raise roughly €90 million to €115 million a year more than the existing system, allowing for a reduction in the current €160 price. Richard Bruton in 2019 promised such a charge to arrive by 2024. It never did.

UK culture secretary Lisa Nandy and her Irish counterpart Patrick O’Donovan face essentially the same problems. But O’Donovan’s are far worse and that, for all RTÉ’s faults, owes less to the broadcaster than to the short-termism and procrastination of successive Irish governments.

I have paid my TV licence long after I needed to. But RTÉ is testing my patience

A universal media charge would be politically unpopular and is regarded by some as regressive. It is far from clear that the organisations themselves have the capacity to remain relevant in the post-broadcast age.

TV licence fee ‘extremely difficult’ to collect if evaders not prosecuted, says RTÉ boss Kevin Bakhurst

Once again, the famous line from The Leopard sums it up. If we want things to stay as they are, things will have to change.

E-fuels are alternatives to oil that are produced using green electricity, carbon dioxide and water.

The carbon-neutral products can be used in existing engines, offering a potential solution to aviation and shipping, which are challenging to electrify, Galetech said on Tuesday.

Under the deal’s terms, Galetech will use Skytree’s systems for capturing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere to use in the fuels.

The company will deploy its Dutch partner’s direct air capture technology, which extracts carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, in its renewable energy businesses in Ireland and Kenya, according to a statement.

Skytree originally developed its technology for the European Space Agency.

Last year, Galetech announced plans to build a pilot e-fuels research and production facility at its Edrans wind farm in Cootehill, Co Cavan, which will produce 100 per cent renewable, synthetic alternatives to petrol, diesel and kerosene.

Skytree’s technology will allow Galetech “develop a truly reliable and sustainable supply chain for renewable fuels”, he said.

Bermingham added that the fuels would be a critical resource for airlines and shipping and transport companies seeking to cut their dependence on fossil fuels.

Skytree’s vice-president, project development, Peter van Hooft, noted that carbon dioxide in the atmosphere can be turned into a valuable ingredient for fuel, rather than “a problem we leave behind”.

]]>KIRAN RIDLEY<![CDATA[Across-the-board pay rise will do little to help fill key public sector posts]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/26/across-the-board-pay-rise-will-do-little-to-help-fill-key-public-sector-posts/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/26/across-the-board-pay-rise-will-do-little-to-help-fill-key-public-sector-posts/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 05:38:00 +0000

Until the early 1970s, the Civil Service was a very traditional organisation that had changed little over time. There was limited movement between departments, and almost none between the public sector and the private sector.

Most people joined straight after school, there were few graduates, although many ambitious civil servants, like TK Whitaker, studied for a degree at night. Unless they were women who married [and who were effectively fired as a result], civil servants were likely to stay until they retired. Men progressed slowly through the ranks, based on seniority.

My first boss in the Department of Finance told me that when he joined it in the 1950s, he had calculated, based on the seniority rule and his colleagues’ ages, that he would spend most of his career as an assistant principal before, in the final three years before retirement, being promoted in rapid succession as a principal officer and then assistant secretary. In the event, he served as secretary general of the department for seven years.

Joining the EU meant quite a number of Irish civil servants left to work for the European Commission. The marriage bar ended in July 1973. Gradually, other reforms led to much more fluid movement across the public service.

The wider public service included graduate roles such as secondary teachers, doctors and local-authority engineers. While less than a third of public servants held third-level qualifications in 1970, those who did constituted more than half of the Irish graduate workforce.

All of this made public sector employment rather different from that in the private sector, with limited parallels in terms of pay. To a large extent, public and private sector employers were not competing to attract the same workers.

The advent of mass third level education in Ireland changed things. Few now enter the public sector straight from school. Primary teachers and nurses now have graduate qualifications. Today, three quarters of public sector workers have a third level qualification, but only constitute a third of graduate workers.

There is also greater choice, and substantial movement, between jobs in the public and private sectors. The security of a public sector job does not have the same allure when there is full employment. So the State as an employer needs to compete to attract and retain talent. That means the public sector must pay competitive rates, or some of the most able and ambitious teachers, civil servants, nurses or physiotherapists will seek better pay elsewhere.

Are public sector workers all as badly off as strikes might suggest? This is what the data says

In the run-up to the 2008 economic crash, average pay in the public sector had reached 50 per cent more than in the private sector – an excessive gap.

Following the collapse in the public finances, all public sector workers experienced painful cuts in pay. Over the subsequent decade, public service pay rose more slowly than the private sector. However, over the past few years the relationship has stabilised.

Public service workers are paid, on average, about 30 per cent more than the private sector, but this largely reflects their higher average qualifications.

The Government now needs to deliver a pay increase for public service workers, not because prices are higher but because most other workers are seeing their pay rise. Failure to keep pace with the private sector would see skilled employees leave.

The Department of Finance forecast that average pay across the economy will rise by around 4 per cent this year and next. The budget arithmetic provided for a 3 per cent public pay rise next year, so any higher pay deal will need additional funding.

The expected rise in private sector pay sets a guideline for any public sector pay agreement. If public sector workers are offered significantly more, that could push up taxes, and have knock-on effects on other pay. But if offered significantly less than their private sector counterparts, there could be an exodus of skilled staff for better pay elsewhere.

A public pay deal will be done – and here’s what it will look like

While this sounds fairly straightforward, things are, of course, more complex. Private sector pay deals are generally contingent on increased productivity. That, too, should be the case in the public sector.

Across-the-board pay increases in the public sector won’t address what’s needed to attract workers to some key areas where posts have been hard to fill – in the Naval Service, in special care, in some IT roles.

While a private employer would simply pay more, public pay agreements cannot easily handle such differentiation, but need to find a way to do so. The alternative of filling key roles by outsourcing to consultants is not an ideal one.

]]>Chris Maddaloni<![CDATA[With EU presidency, Ireland has chance to implement digital identity wallet by end of year ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/with-eu-presidency-ireland-has-chance-to-implement-digital-identity-wallet-by-end-of-year/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/with-eu-presidency-ireland-has-chance-to-implement-digital-identity-wallet-by-end-of-year/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 05:27:00 +0000The priorities for Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the EU have been wide in scope across various sections of society, different sectors within the economy, along with competing national or common interests.

Some of those will resolve in due course under the current term, while many will either stall or progress as it passes onto Lithuania and then Greece through 2027.

One long-standing objective and policy priority that falls directly during our watch is the provision for an EU Digital Identity Wallet for all citizens and businesses by December of this year.

This is part of the wider Digital Decade Policy Programme (DDPP), which is the EU’s framework for achieving digital transformation by the end of the decade.

It includes targets in relation to digital skills, digital infrastructure, the digitalisation of businesses, and access to digital public services.

That last (but not least) area essentially involves all key public services being available online with citizens’ digital identity and ability to access services working seamlessly throughout the EU.

The practical applications are complex but the “only once” principle applies throughout, where citizens should not be repeatedly asked by governments or multiple agencies for information already available.

With progress being made on all fronts to various degrees, this is now a defining period for Ireland to help push the digital public services agenda forward for citizens, businesses and State services. Interoperable data should flow freely enough to support everything from mortgage approvals to healthcare records and planning applications.

The main challenge is one that often falls on European or cross-border projects. It comes down to collective co-ordination and consensus. Twenty-seven member states, with as many starting points, governance structures, all building toward the same targets along separate paths that sometimes fail to intersect.

The issues to be resolved don’t solely lie within policy, legal or technological constraints. It is often social where the connectivity falls down. How do people, who each hold a piece of a public problem, find one another, build trust, and produce outcomes that outlast a ministerial photocall or presidential term? The EU and the Irish Government have invested heavily in the building blocks that are needed for this journey. The digital identity wallets, data spaces and cloud platforms already exist.

What is missing is the right people coming together from different corners, knowing how to assemble these blocks in the right way.

Practitioners who have the ability and mindset to move between a Brussels regulation and a rural county council’s operating reality, without treating the two as separate jobs.

Ireland’s role in this during its EU presidency is reflected in a new initiative that will gather the necessary stakeholders to generate those collective solutions for the next phase of Europe’s digital public services roadmap.

To break the roadblocks and unlock the capabilities that can advance these future services, we need to first go back though to an age-old practice. Before internet technology, quantum computing or artificial intelligence were even imagined, Ireland had meitheal.

This was among our oldest social networks and was based on reciprocity, trust and shared responsibilities. Its approach was replicated in similiar forms in different countries: Norway’s dugnad, Finland’s talkoot, Lithuania’s talka, Hungary’s kaláka and the Balkan moba.

Each European tradition reflects the same civic principle that complex problems can be solved when communities pool effort, skills and responsibility. It activated to do work that no single person or household could manage alone.

The main rule being that help given would be returned. This created a social infrastructure and self-enforcing system for dedicating skills exactly when and where they were needed. That practice and principle may be what is needed now to push forward on Ireland and Europe’s digital public services programme.

On November 19th and 20th, Ireland will hold the first Meitheal Digiteach that will bring policy makers, community groups, data designers, delivery practitioners, architects and engineers into the same room to work through the shared challenges, while looking to create practical solutions and connect the diverging tracks on the new Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) rails.

The gathering will not work like a regular conference with the usual panel discussions, keynote addresses and firesides or roundtables. This will be a hands-on exercise for participants with no hierarchy and no spectators.

It is due to be held at a fitting location within the Drogheda Civic Offices which, since its relatively recent refurbishment, now represents a suitable blend of heritage with modern design and functionality. The call is for like-minded citizens and groups to get involved in building the next level of digital public services.

I’d encourage all who have a role to play to join us, as Ireland’s meitheal provides a mechanism that can be passed on to the next custodians of the EU presidency and the subsequent phases of our shared digital public services programme.

Gar Mac Críosta is digital advisor strategy & architecture at the HSE, and co-founder of Meitheal Digiteach 2026

Jerry Fish: ‘I’m a London-born Dub but I discovered most of my DNA is from exactly where I now live’

Is there anything you regret spending money on?

There is plenty I regret spending money on, but that’s the price of an education, in life and the music business. You live and you learn.

Do you haggle over prices?

Not regularly, but it can be fun. I spent time with Bedouins in the Sinai in the 1980s, and they taught me how to haggle. I love the odd bric-a-brac antique, so you’ve got to haggle sometimes. Also, I am a survivor in the music business, and we have to hustle for a living.

Do you invest in shares and/or cryptocurrency?

Nah, I can’t get my head around cryptocurrency. I miss cash.

Do you have a retirement or pension plan?

I have a pension from some money I got to squirrel away once, when I was flush, but it’s been through a financial crash and a pandemic, so it’s not much. I don’t plan to ever retire, though. I have a job that I love doing, and I know I’m very lucky to be doing what I do. I want to keep on working as a full-time day-dreamer and entertainer until the day I die.

What was the last thing you bought, and was it good value for money?

A trip to Cadiz to hang out with an old and dear friend. You can’t put a value on friendship or making memories, because they are priceless. Friendship is surely the most precious commodity.

Have you ever successfully saved up for a relatively big purchase?

Yes, I’m pretty good at knuckling down to get something if it’s something I truly want. I am aware there are many things I can’t afford, but I believe everything starts with a dream. You have to visualise the things you want, then strive and work hard to get them.

Have you ever lost money?

I have lost pretty much everything I had. Strangely, it was one of the best things to have ever happened to me. I think once you survive a fall, it makes you stronger, less concerned or worried about the road ahead. Losing money isn’t the end of the world. Sometimes you need to let it go, look around at what you have and be grateful.

Camille O’Sullivan: ‘I’m terrified of being out of money’

Are you a gambler, and if so, have you ever had a big win?

The biggest gamble I ever took was returning to the music business after the birth of my first child, and it is also my biggest win. I’m lucky to have made a success of doing the thing I love with the support of a beautiful wife and four wonderful children. As far as I’m concerned, that’s winning at bingo!

What are your best and worst habits when it comes to money?

My best and worst habits when it comes to money are quite possibly the same thing: my generosity, giving away my money. I believe in the karmic effect of giving, in that what you give comes back to you multiplied. I have travelled a lot in my life, and I have always managed to hold on to my fare home, usually hidden somewhere on my person.

How much money do you have on you now?

Everybody knows that cash is king. I have €70 on me.

Jerry Fish performs as part of Puca Festival, Trim Castle Hotel, Saturday, October 31st. pucafestival.com

]]>Marc O'Sullivan<![CDATA[What my most embarrassing job interview taught me]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/26/what-my-most-embarrassing-job-interview-taught-me/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/26/what-my-most-embarrassing-job-interview-taught-me/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 05:24:00 +0000The other day, I was chatting with a friend about how we got into journalism when I suddenly remembered my most disastrously embarrassing job interview.

It happened years ago, not long after I arrived in London and spotted an ad for a deputy news magazine editor. The advert was highly detailed. Applicants had to send in an assessment of the publication outlining what worked and what did not, along with compelling cover story ideas.

Having recently edited a national news magazine in Australia, I was full of thoughts. But there was one question in the advert that stumped me. What was my preferred salary?

I asked two other journalists I knew in London, both men, for advice. Each told me to ask for what I had been paid in Sydney, plus more for the abysmal exchange rate and the cost of living in London, which I did.

To my delight, I got an interview. A team of people politely listened as I went on about their magazine, whose editor then took me off to a side room for a further chat. He loved my application, he said, but there was just one thing. How wedded was I to that salary I had mentioned? “Because it’s a lot more than what I’m paid.”

At the time, I was mortified. My face burned. What an idiot I had been to name such an outlandish figure. Why hadn’t I done a better job of researching the going rate for deputy magazine editors?

Today, though, I recall that moment fondly. Women are always being told they cement the gender pay gap by asking for too little in pay negotiations, and there was my younger self, gormlessly doing the opposite.

I also think of how much easier it would have been if that advert had simply listed the salary on offer. That way, I would have known if it was worth my while to apply and everyone else, inside and outside the magazine, would have had a better idea of whether their pay was fair, or if they should demand more. This is, of course, precisely why so many employers do not spell out salaries in public.

For similar reasons, job hunters are often asked to disclose their salary history, even though this is an excellent way to bake in the lower pay endured by so many women, ethnic minorities and others.

Workplace conflict is said to be costing Irish firms €239m annually. What can be done about it?

It’s tough to ask for £50,000 for a job, no matter how well qualified you are, if you have just revealed your last role paid £35,000, which it might have if you had been doing the same work at, say, a charity.

Women were told for years to just “lean in” and become savvier negotiators. Thankfully, this approach is fading as research shows the benefits of policies aimed at fixing the practice of negotiations, instead of fixing the women.

This is why the EU has brought in a directive requiring employers to do two things: tell job seekers about starting salaries or pay ranges, and stop asking them about their pay histories. A number of US states already have such measures, which can help to shrink a gender wage gap that averaged 11 per cent across OECD countries in 2023.

The deadline to put the EU directive into national law was June 2026, but unfortunately many countries have yet to get there. They include Germany, the bloc’s largest economy, where Indeed data shows that less than 15 per cent of job advertisements include explicit pay information. That number plunges for sectors such as banking and finance, which typically have far worse gender pay gaps.

No wonder thousands of women are supporting outfits such as Female X Finance, a five-year-old start-up that aims to help boost women’s careers in the financial industry. Its Dutch co-founders just published their second annual survey of the salaries – and bonuses – being paid in investment banking, M&A, private equity and other fields in the UK and the Netherlands.

HR bosses predict AI will not cause ‘significant reduction’ in employee numbers

How I wish this type of information, and those pay transparency laws, had been around when I answered that magazine advert all those years ago.

If you’re wondering, I never did get the job. It went to an insider, which is probably just as well. I’m sure they did a far better job than I would have done, but I would still like to know how much they were paid. – The Financial Times

]]>rudi_suardi<![CDATA[‘The focus is finding people from Ireland’: The EU’s big ask for new English translators]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/the-focus-is-finding-people-from-ireland-the-eus-big-ask-for-new-english-translators/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/26/the-focus-is-finding-people-from-ireland-the-eus-big-ask-for-new-english-translators/Mon, 26 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000The list of unintended consequences caused by Brexit runs quite long – and reads somewhat smug when compiled on this side of the Irish Sea – but it can be briefly summarised as political upheaval, economic uncertainty and social division.

Aside from the macro-woes, Britain’s formal departure from the European Union in 2020 has also proved a headache for the diplomats and administrators tasked with running EU institutions for more than 450 million citizens.

“We’re constantly getting requests,” says Linda Forde, the head of the European Parliament’s English-language translation unit, as she takes a short break from her duties during a work trip to Dublin.

Draft after draft of legal documents and policy papers arrive in her inbox daily to be distributed among her team of translators and proofreaders – often with same request: “Can you do this for tomorrow? The day after tomorrow?” she says, quoting colleagues based mostly in Brussels, a three-hour train ride away from her office in Luxembourg.

English, while officially of equal status alongside the EU’s 23 other languages, carries more weight than most because of its status as a “pivot language”.

The term is not easily defined, so Forde provides an example: “Legislation comes in Romanian, we translate it into English and then, for example, the Irish unit will translate it from English because they will not be able to translate it from Romanian.”

The parliament’s translation service employs more than 1,100 people. A standard translation unit is made up of about 30 staff members, but the English unit is among the smallest. This is partly because many texts are originally drafted in English and do not require translation, but the unit’s small size is also a product of its time.

Recruiting translators from Britain has been “problematic” since Brexit, Forde says, due to the EU’s policy of employing strictly its own citizens. The only Britons who can bypass this rule are those with dual citizenship from an EU member state.

“With Ireland being the biggest English-speaking country [in the EU], definitely the focus is finding people from Ireland, because they’re native speakers and that’s what we’re looking for,” says Forde, who is from Co Antrim.

Ireland faces ‘significant’ loss of influence in EU institutions due to retirements

The career translator was in Dublin in early October to speak at an outreach event at the European Parliament’s Liaison Office close to Grafton Street, organised as part of the State’s six-month presidency of the Council of the EU.

Between panel discussions and Q&A sessions, the European Parliament’s director general for translation, Valter Mavric, spoke to The Irish Times about the need for Irish-citizen, English-language translators in the institution.

Irish people “are the only ones that actually can apply. Not formally, not officially, but practically”, the Slovenian man, who is also fluent in Italian, says.

“Theoretically, a Slovenian who has excellent English and has maybe studied in an English-speaking country, might be able to apply. But what’s more important with English, for example, is that you translate the laws or communications for citizens of Ireland primarily.

“So you have to know the Irish version of English,” Mavric says. “That’s why it’s very important to have English native speakers from Ireland.”

‘If you want to get a job immediately in Brussels, speak Irish and do a law degree’

They may well be important to have, but are they difficult to get?

“I think there might be many reasons, before I reply to you, whether it’s difficult or not,” he says in the Robert Schuman breakout room, named after the French elder statesman credited for his role in rebuilding postwar Europe.

Irish citizens “don’t want to leave their country”, he notes, “maybe because it’s so beautiful to live here”. High salaries on offer at home don’t help either, he says.

“Still, we do not have many problems with attracting Irish citizens – we have not had, let’s say it like that, so far,” Mavric adds.

However, “the English team is not complete ... because there are still some colleagues from the UK that work there [since] before Brexit and so they have stayed. But of course, someday these colleagues will retire or will leave and we have to think of succession planning already.”

This is what brought him to Dublin: “We are here this week to promote both English and Irish as the two official languages – for me, it is very important to get that message across.”

Both languages face similar challenges in attracting qualified candidates from Ireland to the highly competitive application process called “translator competitions”, which require applicants to prove fluency in three European languages.

Why foreign governments are paying lobbyists to make their case in Brussels

“Deficiency in knowledge of foreign languages” is the main concern, Mavric says.

Data from the European Commission shows the proportion of Irish secondary school students learning two or more foreign languages was the lowest in the EU, at just 5.2 per cent. In 10 countries, such as Finland and Italy, the proportion was more than 90 per cent.

It appears to be an uphill battle for Ireland to reach the heights of trilingualism, but Mavric is optimistic.

“For me, language is always linked to an identity, to a culture, and that’s why it’s so important to include language as the conditions for the European Union, for the European project. Languages, as part of our lives in Europe, are here to stay.”

   <description>Mehrere chinesische Sponsoren haben am Dienstag das Ende der Zusammenarbeit mit dem französischen Fußballstar Kylian Mbappe verkündet. Er soll mit Äußerungen über Revolutionsführer Mao Zedong (1893–1976) die Gefühle der Chinesen verletzt haben. Eine Entschuldigung des Real-Madrid-Stürmers ließ nicht lange auf sich warten. The United States has chosen Poland to host a new centre for servicing and maintaining missiles used in Patriot air defence systems, in a decision described as “historic” by both Washington and Warsaw. It was chosen ahead of bids from four other European countries, including Germany.

The new centre will “dramatically shorten turnaround times and further secure critical supply lines”, said the US Department of War, announcing the decision on Tuesday.

Undersecretary of War Michael P. Duffey added that the choice of a country on NATO’s eastern front “sends a clear message [that] the Alliance is united, serious about deterrence, and ready to back our words with action”.

Poland Selected to Host Historic PAC-3 Missile Maintenance Facility, Strengthening Allied Burden-Sharing and Transatlantic Security – U.S. Department of War – Release | @DeptofWar https://t.co/2caqADRRx8

— US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) October 27, 2026

The decision was welcomed by Polish leaders, with defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz saying that it shows “Poland is a trusted ally and holds an extremely important place on the map of global security”.

His deputy minister, Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, said that Poland was chosen ahead of rival bids from Germany, the Netherlands and Norway to host the facility. However, US ambassador to Poland Thomas Rose indicated that Sweden, not Norway, was the fourth candidate.

Kosiniak-Kamysz and Sobkowiak-Czarnecka both pointed to the role President Karol Nawrocki had played in securing the deal. On many issues, the government is in conflict with the opposition-aligned president, but the two sides worked together on the Patriot bid.

Historyczna decyzja! Centrum serwisowania pocisków PAC-3 do systemów Patriot powstanie w Polsce! 🇵🇱

O europejską lokalizację tej inwestycji rywalizowały cztery państwa, obok Polski – Niemcy, Holandia i Norwegia. Już na etapie składania wniosków polska oferta została oceniona… pic.twitter.com/wUgFhzlzUk

— Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) October 27, 2026

Nawrocki, a conservative, is a close ally of his US counterpart, Donald Trump. The Polish president’s national security advisor, Bartosz Grodecki, claimed that it was “thanks to a conversation between” the two presidents that the new Patriot servicing centre was being established in Poland.

The head of Nawrocki’s foreign policy office, Marcin Przydacz, meanwhile, thanked Washington for choosing Poland to host the new centre.

“The Polish-American alliance and the good atmosphere in relations once again yield results,” he declared. “We can see what positive effects the President’s activity brings for Poland.”

 

Poland is one of a number of European countries that operate Patriot air defence systems. Others include Germany, Greece, the Netherlands, Romania, Sweden and Ukraine.

The new centre will service the PAC-3 missiles used in Patriot batteries. The competition to host the facility was announced in July, with the selection made by the US government in conjunction with American defence giant Lockheed Martin, the producer of missiles.

In its press release, the Pentagon emphasised that, although Poland would host the new centre, its work would “be underpinned by robust, transatlantic industrial cooperation, with critical supply chain integration led by Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden”.

Sweden will deploy Patriot air defence systems and around 100 accompanying military personnel to Poland later this year to protect the NATO logistics hub in the city of Rzeszów, which is the main conduit for aid to Ukraine https://t.co/cq9p7OVO7E

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 6, 2026

Global demand for Patriot systems has risen significantly, with the United States expending at least 1,500 interceptors in its war with Iran, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

Patriot systems have also been crucial in Ukraine’s defence against Russian ballistic missile attacks, although Ukraine’s supply of missiles is now almost entirely exhausted.

After Trump recently suggested that he would authorise Ukraine to produce its own missiles, Poland offered to host any such factory, to ensure its security. However, today’s announcement concerns a site for maintaining and servicing, rather than producing, the missiles.

Poland has proposed that, if the United States grants Ukraine permission to produce its own missiles for Patriot air-defence systems, the facility could be located on Polish territory to ensure its security https://t.co/jaQng5wtGg

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 28, 2026

The decision cements Poland’s position as one of Washington’s most important security partners in Europe. War secretary Pete Hegseth has praised Poland as a “model ally”, noting that it has for years met NATO’s defence spending targets, unlike many other member states.

Poland has also been a significant customer for US defence firms. Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was NATO’s biggest arms importer, with 44% of the equipment it purchased coming from American suppliers.

Last year, Poland signed a $2 billion deal for the US to provide logistical support and training for Patriot systems. This year, it was announced that Polish state defence group PGZ would become the first European producer of American Barracuda-500M cruise missiles.

Poland will become the first country in Europe to produce cruise missiles developed by US defence firm Anduril Industries

The agreement will "transform the continent's defence industry", claims Anduril https://t.co/LPJnwOLfp2

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026

Warsaw is also currently lobbying for a new permanent US military base to be established in Poland, with the government and the president once again putting aside their differences to promote the idea.

Last month, Nawrocki claimed that the proposed base, which he said would be called “Fort Trump”, was “confirmed”. However, Washington has not publicly announced any final decision.

Germany’s economy minister, Katherina Reiche, has praised Poland as an “example of great success”, saying that it offers a model for other countries.

Speaking at the fourth Polish-German Economic Forum in Warsaw, which she opened on Monday alongside Polish finance minister Andrzej Domański, Reiche. Reiche highlighted the deepening trade ties between the two countries.

She noted that bilateral trade last year exceeded €180 billion for the first time, up from €25 billion in 2000, reports Deutsche Welle.

Germany has been Poland’s biggest trading partner for decades, although recent data suggest that China, for the first time in history, overtook Germany as Poland’s largest source of imports in July this year.

Germany has also long been a major investor in Poland. But Reiche welcomed growing recent investments by Polish companies in Germany, which she said was helping to create jobs.

Earlier this year, for example, Poland’s largest manufacturer of trains and trams, Pesa, announced the acquisition of German rival HeiterBlick as part of its efforts to expand its operations across Europe.

Reiche noted that around 1,000 Polish companies have invested in Germany while about 1,600 German companies have invested in Poland, reports Reuters.

Poland’s largest manufacturer of trains and trams, Pesa, has announced the acquisition of German rival HeiterBlick as it seeks to expand its operations across Europe https://t.co/N1wE1aYL5m

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 12, 2026

Among leading German firms with a presence in Poland are carmakers Mercedes-Benz, which recently invested around €1 billion to build its first electric-only van plant there, which produces its Crafer vans at a plant near the city of Poznań.

Reiche also pointed to Poland’s stellar economic performance since joining the European Union in 2004, noting that its GDP has grown by an annual average of 3.8% over that period – twice the EU-wide average.

Poland’s economy is on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to become part of the G20.

 

Meanwhile, Domański used his remarks at the Polish-German Economic Forum to warn Europe against repeating past mistakes as it confronts a rapidly changing geopolitical landscape.

He said the continent faced a “unique” historical moment. “The world is changing faster than ever, and we are facing new geopolitical, strategic, and technological challenges.”

Europe would need a strong economy and new sources of growth to meet those challenges, he added, warning against what he called “economic naivety” and urging Europe – and Germany in particular – not to return to its previous approach to Russia.

“I would like to state this very clearly: Europe must learn from the past. Under no circumstances can there be a return to the previous approach toward Russia. Poland will never agree to that,” Domański said, noting that this position applied in particular to renewed use of Russian energy imports.

“We will only be resilient once we are truly independent of external, unstable suppliers of raw materials,” he added, emphasising that Poland and Germany must “work together to modernise the European energy market, focus on technological change and bear security in mind”.

Debata ministra @Domanski_Andrz i minister @BMWE_ Katherina Reiche podczas IV Polsko-Niemieckiego Forum Gospodarczego.
💬 Powinniśmy skupić się na cenach energii, ale potrzebne jest znacznie bardziej zdecydowane podejście do ochrony rynku europejskiego. I nie chodzi tu tylko o… pic.twitter.com/NVPUjwx7jA

Following the forum, Domański and Reiche attended a meeting of the Friends of Industry, an informal initiative bringing together EU member states to coordinate positions on industrial policy, competitiveness and the operating conditions for European industry.

The findings come shortly after parliament approved legislation intended to ease access to abortion. But the measures face a potential veto from right-wing, opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki.

In 2020, Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means pregnancies can now only be legally terminated in two cases: where they result from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if they threaten the mother’s life or health.

In a new poll by SW Research for Rzeczpospolita, a leading newspaper, a total of 67.2% of respondents said that they want to liberalise that law. However, only 37.7% favoured introducing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy.

Meanwhile, 29.5% preferred the softer option of returning to the situation from before the 2020 TK ruling – often referred to the “abortion compromise” in Poland – in which terminations were only available in three cases.

 

A further 16.2% supported maintaining the current abortion law; 6.0% wanted to make the rules even tougher (which would involve removing one or both justifications for abortion that currently exist); and 10.6% said they had no opinion.

The poll found that support for liberalisation of abortion was stronger among women (73.8%) than men (60.3%).

The latest findings are consistent with previous polling, which tends to show that a significant majority supports liberalising the abortion law but that there is not a majority in favour of abortion on demand (although some individual polls have narrowly found such a majority).

However, more conservative elements of the government, especially the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), prefer a return to the pre-2020 “compromise”.

Much of the right-wing opposition, meanwhile, favours maintaining the status quo. However, some more moderate elements of the opposition have suggested it would be best to reverse the TK ruling and return to the “compromise”.

By Philipp Fritz, Warsaw correspondent for Die Welt (which first published this article in German here)

Negotiations on compensation for the still-living victims of the German occupation of Poland have been going on for years. There are some 30,000 to 50,000 such survivors, but their number dwindles every week. Berlin should act now.

No “humanitarian gesture” has emerged. “The draft budget currently reflects the fact that no decision has been made,” said Josef Hinterseher, a German foreign office spokesman, at a press conference in late September.

He thereby confirmed what many observers had suspected: survivors of concentration camps, ghettos and death marches, former forced workers and participants in the Warsaw Uprising who are still living in Poland will not receive any compensation, one-off payment or monthly pension from the German government.

The German chancellor has announced that his country will offer support to surviving Polish victims of WW2 and will help strengthen Poland’s eastern border.

However, in both cases he did not provide details of what these measures will involve in practice https://t.co/gKX6142Alo

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2024

Just a few sentences later, Hinterseher moved onto the next subject – the fact that two Russian oligarchs were to be removed from the EU’s sanctions list. Or at least, that Berlin had not been successful in opposing this decision.

The fact that these two issues were dealt with publicly one after the other shows that the German government is quicker to reach a decision that makes Putin’s supporters’ lives easier than it is with victims of the Nazi terror. It is a declaration of moral bankruptcy.

Warsaw and Berlin have been negotiating compensation for the last remaining victims of the German occupation of Poland for years. There are between 30,000 and 50,000 of them – aged over 90, often living alone and in poor health. Their numbers are dwindling every week.

The fact that talks are taking place in Berlin ministries but without any decision being taken is met with sadness and fury in Poland.

 

Increasingly, Poles are getting the impression that, even if the Germans manage to put up memorials, they cannot offer survivors tangible help when it is asked for. It is a common view that in Berlin the descendants of the perpetrators are simply waiting for the victims to die so that this pesky issue will sort itself out.

Should that happen, those left behind will not forget, and the Germans will hardly be able to forgive themselves.

Warsaw is no longer demanding war reparations from Berlin. In December 2023, Donald Tusk’s government switched to talking about “making amends”.

Polish foreign minister @sikorskiradek has called on Germany to “think creatively” about compensating Poland for WWII.

On a visit to Berlin, he also said that the new government would "end the cold war" waged by the former ruling PiS party against Germany https://t.co/kZ62nUuqqO

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 31, 2024

This is not just splitting hairs. In so doing, Tusk put the ball in the German government’s court, giving it the chance to take action and, through a gesture recognising suffering and providing a relatively small sum of money, to offer people tangible help and do a service to the German-Polish relationship.

Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz is reported to have offered Tusk a one-off payment in 2024, but Poland’s prime minister turned the sum down as insufficient. Instead, Polish diplomats are demanding monthly pensions.

In any case, we are talking about a few hundred million euro: a relatively small amount compared to the equivalent of €1.3 trillion that Poland’s former ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party once demanded from Germany, and also in comparison to many other budget items – and yet still there is nothing about compensation in the budget planning.

Poland is seeking $1.3 trillion in war reparations from Germany, but Berlin says the issue was legally settled long ago.

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 9, 2022

Rumour has it that, in return for compensation, German foreign ministry officials are asking for a kind of Polish guarantee that in future there will be no more demands for reparations, or at least that at least the German gesture will receive good press in Poland.

If that is true, it would be thoroughly indecent, bringing to mind an image of a perpetrator trying to buy his victim’s silence. This reflects a belief in objectification, an ugly bureaucratic mentality stemming from a system in which “work” in a ghetto counts towards statutory pension contributions, but no one can bring themselves to pay compensation.

This issue can be resolved at the very top. Chancellor Friedrich Merz would have to work with the relevant ministries – the foreign office and finance ministry – to provide for compensation for the victims in the budget. This would be a belated but major and morally right gesture. If politics is too slow – time really is of the essence – then civil society should take it upon itself to show where it stands.

Donations for the still living victims of the German tyranny or a fund from which survivors would receive monthly payments can be created from within society. Business can also get involved. German corporations which were guilty of, for instance, exploiting forced labourers in occupied Poland, or those that emerged from them, such as BASF, Siemens, Volkswagen, BMW and Deutsche Bank, could contribute.

By Aleks Szczerbiak

Political scandals generate intense media attention and public outrage but rarely produce dramatic shifts in party support that they once did.

They are now more likely to affect electoral outcomes indirectly by demobilising softer, less committed voters and influencing turnout, particularly among supporters of the government disappointed by its apparent underperformance and broken election promises.

The hospital scandal

Two high-profile political scandals dominated the Polish news agenda for much of this summer. The first centred on irregularities at Warsaw’s Southern Hospital (Szpital Południowy) and involved a young and relatively inexperienced doctor, Dawid Kacprzyk.

In spite of his lack of a specialist qualification, Kacprzyk coordinated the hospital’s emergency department and reportedly earned a staggering 1.6 million złoty (€366,000) in the previous year alone. He also served as a Warsaw district councilor for the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) grouping, Poland’s main governing party led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Public outrage intensified following reports that the hospital had operated a dedicated “VIP path” or special lounge where ruling-party-linked politicians and their families were allowed faster access and medical examinations without the usual queues faced by ordinary patients.

Further claims emerged, including a whistleblower surgeon alleging that supervisory failures contributed to patient deaths and of improper private business activity in the hospital morgue.

Poland’s health minister has unveiled a set of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in public hospitals following a series of reports about exorbitant pay for some doctors and that politically connected patients could skip queues and use a "VIP lounge" https://t.co/pidAHxohc4

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026

For its part, KO insisted that the scandal was the personal misconduct of one former party member rather than a general problem affecting the entire healthcare system. They noted that Kacprzyk quickly resigned his council seat and hospital role, and that party-aligned Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski had dismissed the hospital board and two of his deputy mayors overseeing the city’s health services.

KO argued that no specific names of preferential VIP patients had been publicly confirmed, any irregularities were being fully investigated by prosecutors and independent bodies, and political and legal accountability would follow if ethical breaches or crimes were proven. The government also pledged systemic reforms including measures to curb excessive pay for doctors.

Nonetheless, the scandal struck a deep chord with the Polish public, triggering massive negative media and political fallout that aligned perfectly with the right-wing opposition’s narrative painting KO as part of a “Warsaw elite” that enjoys special privileges at the expense of ordinary citizens.

The cryptocurrency scandal

The second major summer scandal centred on allegations of financial impropriety and political entanglement involving Zondacrypto, once Poland’s largest crypto trading platform, that claimed over a million users but earlier this year collapsed abruptly after thousands of retail investors were unable to access their funds.

However, what began as a major financial scandal escalated into political warfare, providing the government with powerful ammunition to attack the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, party-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, and the broader conservative political eco-system over payments and donations made by the crypto firm.

Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a collapsed crypto firm, of organisations and individuals linked to the right-wing opposition, including the Polish version of US conservative conference CPAC https://t.co/swceV864nA

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 26, 2026

For example, Zondacrypto sponsored the 2025 Polish edition of the Conservative Political Action Committee (CPAC) conference attended by the then-presidential candidate Nawrocki, advertised heavily with conservative media outlets such as the TV Republika television network, and made donations to foundations linked to high-ranking PiS figures such as former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro.

The government also tried to entangle Nawrocki, who repeatedly vetoed its cryptocurrency regulation laws, into the scandal, arguing that he was protecting the shady interests of the industry and its political beneficiaries at the expense of ordinary Poles (the Tusk administration lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority required to overturn a presidential veto).

For their part, PiS and the broader Polish right dismissed the government’s accusations as a smear campaign and sought to shift blame for the scandal onto the Tusk administration for inadequate oversight to protect investors. Figures on the right, including those connected to foundations that received money, framed these dealings as legitimate sponsorships common across the media and other organisations.

The president of the Polish Olympic Committee has been detained as part of a criminal investigation into Zondacrypto, a crypto firm that collapsed earlier this year and was a major sponsor of Poland's Olympic team https://t.co/QPG7ejAImD

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 27, 2026

PiS rejected claims that the party or associated groups received funds from the firm and defended Nawrocki’s vetoes as necessary against flawed legislation.

Nonetheless, opinion polls found that most respondents linked the scandal to PiS and the right-wing opposition, providing the government with numerous attack lines to force them onto the defensive.

The diminishing impact of scandals

It is worth recalling how an earlier era of post-communist politics scandals possessed much greater transformative, system-altering capacity and could act as catalysts for the restructuring of the electoral landscape.

For example, at the beginning of the 2000s, the so-called “Rywin scandal” was widely seen as a decisive factor in the near-destruction as a political force of the previously powerful, and then-governing, communist-successor Democratic Left Alliance (SLD). The scandal erupted in late 2002 when film producer Lew Rywin allegedly solicited a large bribe from the Agora media group, publisher of the influential liberal-left Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper, in exchange for media legislation changes while claiming to act on behalf of a “group holding power” (grupa trzymająca władzę) linked to the ruling party.

A high-profile parliamentary investigative commission, sustained media focus, and a series of follow-on scandals and accumulation of allegations of deep-seated influence peddling by post-communist networks created a powerful narrative of systemic bribery and corruption, completely discrediting the SLD as a competent governing force.

Having won a substantial victory in the 2001 parliamentary election, securing 41% of the votes, its support collapsed to only 11% at the next 2005 poll. This helped clear the way for the rise of the KO (originally Civic Platform)-PiS duopoly that has structured the Polish party system ever since, thereby establishing a precedent that scandals were electorally fatal transgressions.

 

The contrast with the recent hospital and cryptocurrency scandals is instructive and illustrates a broader transformation in the relationship between political misconduct and electoral politics in Poland.

Whereas in the more fluid party system of the early post-communist period a cluster of major scandals or single-event shocks could rapidly destroy dominant parties and restructure competition, now – although they still generate intense, high-octane political and media outrage – such controversies appear to slide off the main political actors with remarkably little immediate consequence.

Indeed, neither of these recent scandals produced the dramatic shift in headline polling numbers that some observers, drawing on historical precedent, might have anticipated given the intensity of the media coverage.

Scandal-neutralising structural shifts

This change stems from three interlocking shifts in the structural dynamics of Poland’s political system. Taken together, they have substantially diminished the capacity of scandals to move headline poll numbers and trigger the kind of large-scale systemic realignments seen in an earlier era of post-communist politics.

Firstly, the sheer velocity of modern political communication prevents single-issue-based scandals from sustaining public focus. In the early 2000s, a major corruption scandal could dominate the news headlines for months through concentrated media attention. The Rywin scandal unfolded through prolonged televised parliamentary commission hearings, keeping the story alive and allowing public outrage to build into a sustained narrative that slowly drained the ruling party’s legitimacy.

Today, digital algorithms and the 24-hour news cycle ensure that a major story, whether about healthcare management or cryptocurrency, moves at a breathtaking pace and is overtaken rapidly as public attention moves onto the next domestic controversy, international development, or strategic counter-narrative.

Seven people have been charged in relation to alleged corruption in the issuing of Polish visas to foreign nationals

The scandal has engulfed the government since last week, but officials say the opposition is exaggerating the scale and nature of the case https://t.co/iHnIShb1pQ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2023

This hyper-accelerated news cycle means that even a high-profile case that generates intense short-term media coverage does not remain the dominant story for long enough to produce cumulative, system-level damage by limiting the time window in which a scandal can convert temporary disapproval into lasting shifts in voting intentions. Scandals thereby become a form of ambient “background noise” in Polish public life rather than a singular focal point for popular outrage.

Secondly, and perhaps most formidably, the protective shield of deep polarisation and socio-political division renders large segments of the electorate relatively impervious to allegations against “their” side. After 2005, the Polish party system crystallised around a durable “post-transition” socio-economic divide reinforced by cultural and geopolitical fault lines.

In this deeply fractured and highly polarised landscape, with large segments of the electorate embedded within hostile camps, when a scandal like the hospital crisis or cryptocurrency controversy breaks, voters interpret allegations levelled against “their” party through a tribal filter as a politically motivated hit job or the work of hostile media.

So even severe scandals are shaped by, and largely confirm, existing political loyalties and rarely trigger cross-camp voter defections. This is a sharp contrast with the early 2000s, when the party system was still fluid and electoral volatility high.

Our essential guide to Poland's parliamentary elections, which will take place one year from now.

How does voting work? What do polls suggest the outcome will be? Which issues may animate the campaign? And what role will President Nawrocki play? https://t.co/fmdoFpBaxz

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026

Thirdly, the parties themselves have become far more professional at message discipline and crisis management. Today’s parties are centralised media machines staffed by sophisticated public relations strategists who view a scandal not as a moral crisis but a communication problem requiring aggressive damage containment.

Rather than allowing a controversy to fester, they immediately launch counterattacks, accusing their opponents of far greater historical or concurrent corruption, and ruthlessly enforce internal party discipline and message conformity.

They also deploy well-rehearsed crisis management playbooks including: personnel sanctions; framing the problem as local or individual responsibility, or residual rather than systemic failure; ordering visible audits, investigations, or reforms to demonstrate “taking action”; and co-ordinated messaging that seeks to close the story quickly and shift the focus back onto the other side’s weaknesses or broader policy issues.

Differential mobilisation, not voter persuasion

Yet while polarisation and professional crisis management allow parties to survive the immediate news cycle, this does not mean that scandals have become irrelevant. Rather, their effects are more subtle and delayed through the “slow-burn” mechanism of differential turnout by selectively demobilising specific voter segments.

Although in a highly polarised polity the most committed hard-core partisans are relatively immune to negative information about “their” side, soft or conditional supporters may become disillusioned, or simply less motivated, when repeated scandals reinforce a narrative of self-interest or incompetence.

The net result is a gradual, cumulative, asymmetric demobilisation of one camp that does not fully register in standard inter-election voting intention surveys, which generally show expressed party preferences among those willing to answer but not necessarily the intensity of that preference or the probability that a respondent will actually turn out to vote.

In Poland’s deeply polarised political landscape, the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, is unlikely to be determined by persuading voters to cross the ideological divide. Rather differential levels of electoral turnout and mobilisation are likely to be the key, specifically: whichever side’s core base is more motivated to – and peripheral, less ideologically committed “softer” supporters are demotivated from – showing up on polling day.

Young Poles are bucking the international trend by turning out at a higher rate than the oldest voters in recent elections.

We spoke with experts and young voters to find out more about the growing frustrations that are driving this political engagement https://t.co/y1JpYYmbjb

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025

And in a context where the election is likely to be closely fought, and relatively small differences in participation rates could prove decisive, although they may not produce dramatic changes in headline party polling preferences, scandals can still play a significant role. However, we are only likely to see the full impact of any such scandals when voters eventually go to the polls and actual turnout patterns are revealed.

Given the general disillusionment with the current government and growing narrative of its underperformance and failure to deliver on its electoral promises, scandals are more likely to contribute to the demobilisation of the governing camp. It is anyway inherently more difficult for incumbent parties to mobilise their disillusioned supporters to turn out and vote than it is for motivated oppositions to rally their base to oust them.

Indeed, revealed voter preferences in the summer 2025 presidential election – when Nawrocki won an unexpected victory over Trzaskowski, the ruling party-backed favourite – and more recently the severe setback for KO in the Kraków mayoral by-election, suggest that government supporters are already showing greater reluctance to vote.

So, while their effects are routinely neutralised by fast-moving news, tribal shielding and professional spin, scandals still matter in Polish politics, although the battleground has shifted from voter persuasion to differential mobilisation.

The UK government is considering forcing data centre developers to invest in local communities and meet sustainability targets in exchange for priority access to the grid, as ministers miss their own deadline for introducing new planning rules.

Under proposals being examined ahead of Wednesday’s Budget, developers could be required to make financial contributions to local areas or meet energy-use standards in return for faster planning approvals or grid connections.

The proposed ‘data centre covenant’, first reported by the Financial Times, comes as ministers attempt to triple Britain’s computing capacity to six gigawatts by 2030, despite growing pressure on the electricity network.

The government has already brought data centres into the Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects regime, allowing major developments to be considered through a national planning process.

But ministers have missed their own deadline to consult on the National Policy Statement intended to guide those decisions.

The government committed in November 2025 to launching a consultation within three months, but the February deadline passed without the proposals being published.

In a recent parliamentary answer, AI minister Kanishka Narayan said the statement would be published “in due course”.

The policy will establish how major data centres should be designed and their environmental impacts managed, while ministers are also considering granting the infrastructure Critical National Priority status.

Grid delays threaten investment

The proposals come as electricity shortages increasingly threaten Britain’s efforts to attract investment from major tech firms.

Last week, Microsoft withdrew from plans to build Britain’s largest AI data centre in Loughton, Essex, after grid constraints prevented the project from securing power for its planned 2026 opening.

Britain’s electricity connection queue surged from 41GW in November 2024 to 125GW by June 2025, according to Ofgem, with data centres accounting for at least 80GW of applications.

The government has sought to address the backlog through its proposed Great British Grid, which would allow businesses to build more of their own electricity connections.

Meanwhile, growing opposition to data centre construction has raised questions about whether local communities are benefiting from the investment.

An investigation published on Tuesday by Spotlight on Corruption found that senior government officials met 137 businesses while developing the country’s AI Growth Zones policy, compared with just two community groups and no environmental organisations.

A taskforce involving Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco recently warned ministers that Britain had roughly 12 months to prevent US-style opposition from disrupting data centre construction.

The government has already announced that councils hosting data centres in AI Growth Zones will be able to retain additional business rates generated by the developments.

The proposed covenant could go further by tying planning and grid access directly to commitments from developers, although its final terms have yet to be agreed.
