WITH the domestic jumps action difficult to weigh up this weekend, I’m looking across the pond to hunt out a few ante-post picks from the Breeders’ Cup.

The two-day extravaganza from Keeneland in Lexington, Kentucky kicks off on Friday evening with a card for the juveniles before Saturday night’s action sees the older champions crowned.

Charlie Appleby will be hoping that he can pull off a famous double with NOTABLE SPEECH in the Grade One Breeders’ Cup Mile (8.20pm).

His globe-trotting son of Dubawi was a brilliant winner of this race 12 months ago, when Del Mar played host to the Breeders’ Cup.

On that occasion he showed his electric turn of foot around the tight turns of the Californian circuit, and the quick ground expected at Keeneland should be right up his alley again.

Notable Speech has an excellent record when sent over to North America, winning three times and placing one from five trips, including last time when landing the Grade One Woodbine Mile in Canada.

He also has previous experience of Keeneland and, while he’s short at 11/10 with Paddy Power, he should take plenty of beating in what is likely to be his final start before retirement.

Also in the Mile, I can’t resist a small each-way play on FACTEUR CHEVAL.

This seven-year-old contested many of the world’s top mile and 10-furlong races when trained in France by Jerome Reynier, and landed Group One honours in the 2024 Dubai Turf.

Earlier this month, he transferred to Canadian trainer Mark Casse and won his first start for his new handler over an extended mile at Keeneland.

US-style racing could suit him, and it wouldn’t be a massive surprise to see a big run at 50/1 with William Hill.

There’s an enthralling clash between Nunthorpe winner BACIO and July Cup victor Comanche Brave in the Grade One Breeders’ Cup Turf Sprint (5.48pm).

US trainer Wesley Ward brought Bacio over to the UK for the summer and he triumphed at Royal Ascot before taking the step up to Group One company in the Nunthorpe.

He showed blazing speed to put his rivals to the sword from the stalls at York, and from a good draw in stall three this race looks ideally set up for him to employ similar tactics.

While Comanche Brave has been impressive this season, he has it to prove against Bacio in his own backyard.

A price of 11/8 may look short on the face of it, but ante-post betting is all about value, and I think Bacio could be odds-on come Saturday.

Blue Bolt sets a high standard in the Grade One Breeders’ Cup Filly & Mare Turf (7.04pm).

However, I’ve a feeling JANCIS could be ideally suited to this one-mile-one-and-a-half-furlong trip.

Willie McCreery’s mare looked the winner last time out in the Grade One E. P. Taylor Stakes at Woodbine, only to fade in the final half-furlong and finish a close third.

She steps back a half-furlong in trip here, and looks suited to running around a bend on quick ground.

Jancis was only just over a length behind Blue Bolt at Royal Ascot, so she must be of interest at 20/1.

Finally, in the Breeders’ Cup Turf (9.36pm), BENVENUTO CELLINI is of interest against his better-fancied stablemate Diamond Necklace.

Ryan Moore would have struggled to do the weight aboard the filly, but Benvenuto Cellini is much better drawn and should be suited to the quick ground at Keeneland.

He’s more than three times the price of Diamond Necklace and appeals as a value each-way play at 6/1.

Netflix insists that Fallon Sherrock and other faces from the PDC circuit were made to queue up and audition alongside thousands of hopefuls before being selected for its new live show, Beat Luke Littler.

The programme has attracted a backlash from darts fans after it was initially billed as a chance for pub players to take on Littler over one leg of 501 in a bid to win £501,000 – only for a series of well-known players to be announced in the line-up last week. 

The standout name is Sherrock, 32, the only woman to win a PDC World Darts Championship match and reach the third round at Alexandra Palace. The live show is due to air this Friday evening, in what is Netflix’s first entry into darts. 

City AM has been told, however, that these “amateurs”, some already well-remunerated from playing competitive darts, still had to wait around in queues for heats in London and Manchester with the part-time players and other genuine amateurs who believed they had a shot, and attend subsequent audition interviews.

A Netflix spokesperson said: “The application and audition process for Beat Luke Littler was exactly the same for everyone and open only to people aged 12 and over who do not hold – and have never held – a PDC Tour Card.

“The final 24 that have been selected for the chance to face Luke this week, all queued up to compete in the heats in London or Manchester, respectively, and managed to complete a leg of 501 in 24 darts or less to prove their darting ability.”

Littler up against Nando’s manager and junior world champion on Netflix show

While the contenders include a Nando’s restaurant manager, a bin collector and former British Army captain, many are PDC-ranked players. Mitchell Lawrie, a 15-year-old Scot tipped to be the next Littler, is a reigning junior world champion, while Ashley Coleman is 34th in the PDC Challenge Tour order of merit.

Insiders argue that none of the contenders currently holds a PDC Tour card, thus making them amateurs. The selection also greatly increases the chances of someone winning the half-a-million-pound prize, given the prospects of someone off the street beating perhaps the greatest darts player in history.

Littler, 19, is already a back-to-back world champion whose meteoric rise has been credited with fuelling the popularity of darts and attracting institutional investment to the sport.

Thousands of family businesses could face being priced out of passing their business down to their offspring should Chancellor John Healey to use his maiden Budget to clamp down on a little-known rule making it easier for firms to transfer ownership.

Treasury officials have been mulling an overhaul of so-called company distribution rules that would make it more attractive for founders to offload their business to private equity than hand it down to the next generation.

One of the options under consideration – making the transfer of a business from one generation to another liable to income tax as opposed to capital gains – has already sparked uproar from entrepreneurs and business owners.

But Chris Etherington, tax partner at RSM, told City AM that the consultation also includes a suite of other proposals that are “much more troubling” than the capital gains tax clampdown. 

One possibility buried in the HMRC plans published in the summer, could see officials dismantle a buyout structure favoured by many retiring entrepreneurs.

Upon retiring, founders’ families rarely have the cash needed to buy their parents out, leading many companies to issue retiring business owners  ‘redeemable preference shares’. 

The share class acts as a bridge, allowing retirees to freeze their financial stake and slowly withdraw capital from the business over time as the firm makes profit. It also allows children to take immediate control of the company.

These deferred repayments are typically treated as parents selling an investment, meaning it is charged as capital gains tax (CGT), between 10 per cent and 24 per cent.

Shifting to dividend tax

But the consultation looked at scrapping this arrangement for staged handovers by no longer recognising the current, real value of the shares being bought back.

Instead, HMRC has proposed capping the returns at the level originally invested by founders when shares were first issued, meaning anything above that baseline will be recognised as an income dividend.

In the majority of cases, the move would cause retirees’ tax bill to nearly double, as higher and additional rate taxpayers will be slapped with dividend taxes of between 35.75 per cent and 39.35 per cent.

On those handing over £1m, the tax bill can swell from £200,000 to roughly £393,00 making it financially unviable for the next generation to pay off their parents without running out of capital or selling the business.

In a response to the consultation, Mark Goddard, tax partner at KPMG, warned that this overhaul could put families at a “disadvantage” to third-parties and ultimately discourage generational ownership.

RSM’s Etherington said that the government is “trying to clamp down” on people who may be trying to take “advantage of the rules to try and get capital gains tax treatment” when it should be income tax, but warned them to be cautious.

“As a government, don’t… throw such a large net over it that you capture innocent scenarios that fundamentally stop businesses from being passed down to the next generation or to third parties in the right way.”

“It could impact management buyouts, it could impact family buyouts, people just wanting to retire. We don’t want to do that. That’s bad for the economy.”

The two-year trap

HMRC is also considering changes to the conditions under which companies can buyback shares from retiring founders.

Under current legislation, businesses can buy back shares through accumulated profit over several years to protect everyday capital, ensuring enough is set aside to pay taxes, suppliers and wages.

But HMRC is debating ending this by introducing a strict two year-cut off time to qualify for capital gains treatment. If a departing founder still holds shares beyond the 24-month window, companies lose the tax break and payments are instead subject to income tax. 

Advisers have warned this leaves businesses highly exposed to supply chain shocks or other problems if they are forced to purchase all shares over the two year window, as it is a much shorter time frame.

HMRC did not respond to a request for comment

Ahead of the Autumn Budget 2026, and the threat of cheaper gherkins for all, Adam Bloodworth on his love for the humble pickled vegetable, which is both delightfully crunchy and a hack to health

My housemate Will has always been the sort of man with impossible levels of fitness. So when I started a new eat-healthier regime, I went to Will with some questions. I didn’t ask how he got muscular (I assumed that would be from lifting weights) – what felt more relatable was to ask him what he was eating. One of the hacks, he said, is gherkins. They have three calories a piece, he told me, beaming, in our kitchen. 

So it was music to my ears when Burnham’s first budget unveiled an unprecedented price-drop for gherkins in the form of a 12 per cent tariff cut for importing them. 

They also have tartness, a light sweetness, and that famously generous crunch. Once the whole gherkin is inserted into your mouth, they require you to eat a bit like a dog, jaw swinging, eyes fixed, to ensure that everything – juice, flesh – is contained. You could cut them in half but where’s the fun in that? These great, cumbersome things are a workout in themselves.

Autumn Budget 2026 and the return of the gherkin

Anyway, try eating a whole jar at once. That’s what I do, on the regular. It’s now it’s become a part of my personality.

There’s no denying that after demolishing a whole vessel, chewing a family’s week-long supply of the vinegary veg, I’m exhausted. As well as embarrassed. But it’s worth it in the end.

Polishing off a whole jar does something to your brain: all that chewing makes you feel like you’ve eaten lots. It’s nature’s Ozempic.

“Higher bond yields help attract the foreign capital the UK needs, but they also raise the government’s interest bill, eroding fiscal headroom and leaving even less space for spending or tax relief,” said Kevin Thozet, portfolio adviser at Carmignac. “The more expensive it becomes to fund the external deficit, the more difficult it becomes to run an expansionary fiscal policy.”

AI has entered the legal world, but rather than making lawyers lazier, it should force them to think harder, writes Alex Fortescue-Webb in today’s Notebook

AI doesn’t have to mean lazier lawyers

Last week the Law Society made it clear that lawyers remain accountable for how juniors use AI. The legal profession is concerned about indiscriminate AI use, understandably given the number of stories of hallucinations that have hit the headlines. A recent HEPI survey found that 94 per cent of undergrads are using AI for assessed work. So when those students become lawyers, they are already familiar with these tools, but how they use them is largely going unchecked.

Clearly, a lot has changed in the last four years. AI tools are now able to competently take on significant amounts of the routine work juniors used to cut their teeth on. That means two things: first, they will have the opportunity to consider strategic issues much earlier in their careers; second, the way they are trained, and their own self-development, will need to evolve.

The first is a huge positive – involvement in the substantive issues of a case, a transaction or indeed any piece of legal work is the reason many students decide to study law in the first place. Their ambitions will now be realised sooner, and their careers are likely to progress faster.

Good training can support this. AI is going to make training much more specific – available in real time or through highly detailed and tailored simulations. At the same time, junior lawyers should treat AI as a thinking partner rather than relying on it – pushing back on its outputs, interrogating reasoning, verifying key sources and, crucially, taking full responsibility for their work.

We also believe that it is going to be critical for future lawyers to start learning how to use AI as a complement to (rather than a replacement for) their own critical thinking – to support that, we’ve expanded our Legal AI Scholars Programme so that students can experiment with Legora while they study.

Linklaters is adopting AI rapidly

The photo was taken at Legal Tech Talk, where I sat down with Sarah Barnard from Linklaters. We talked the room through how Linklaters got lawyers using AI: almost 80 per cent of its partners now use Legora every month – one of the fastest partner adoption ramps either of us has seen. A big part of that was their approach of training a small group of 12 partners, getting them comfortable with the tech before they brought their colleagues up to speed.

Quote of the week

“Always assume positive intent”

Not sure where that came from but it can really change how you interact with people

Mathematical breakthrough

In September, around 10,000 AI agents working in parallel for 88 hours produced a proposed solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems set by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000. Mathematicians have worked on it for decades without success. The proof still needs independent verification, and the Clay Institute waits two years before considering any solution, but it’s a remarkable moment for mathematics that I’ll be following closely.

A book recommendation

Why We Sleep by Matthew Walker is the book I always recommend to people. Walker, a neuroscientist at the University of California, Berkeley, explains what the research tells us about sleep and how it affects almost every part of our health, from memory and learning to mood. It changed how much I prioritise sleep. In a profession where long hours and late nights are often worn as a badge of honour, it makes a convincing case that proper rest is one of the best things you can do for your work.

Alex Fortescue-Webb is head of UK at Legora

Getty’s bankruptcy caps years of damage to editorial photography and freelance livelihoods; its collapse should inspire little sympathy]]>

So Getty Images has filed for bankruptcy. Excuse me while I locate my microscopic mandolin. Oh dear, how sad, never mind. I, for one, will not shed any tears. To misquote Churchill, never have so many photographers owed such a debt of ingratitude to so few. Back in the day we were all shafted by Getty, albeit sometimes unknowingly. 

Getty flew too close to the sun and got burnt – in the process it left a photography industry that’s a shadow of its former self.

Sadly, I’m not blameless. When I was a young picture editor at the Independent and the Independent on Sunday, juggling million-pound budgets while under the cosh of the accountants and the bean counters, Getty offered a solution to my ever-growing problem. It seemed like such a great idea, something so simple that I kicked myself for not thinking of it. A free at the point of delivery monthly contract. No more guessing over reproduction fees or freelance shifts, just a fixed monthly fee. Predictable and budgetable.

An all-you-can-eat Getty binge

Once you had paid, you could binge on the visual delights of all of their photographers and the many agencies they had brought under their vast and terrible umbrella. A veritable buffet of images, a smorgasbord of sports and news. If you had a seat at the table, it was perfect. If not? Well, that was a different story.

The accountants were happy (which meant I was happy) but the freelancers starved. This one bright idea did more to destroy editorial photography than anything before or since, including the advent of AI.

The money fell out of the market, and freelance news photography starved to death. London, once home to a living, breathing, thriving microeconomy of press photographers – an incubator for new talent – died the death of a thousand cuts.

Once it had eaten news photography alive, it moved on to the then very lucrative market of stock photography, buying libraries and agencies with a view to infinite growth, with a fair bit of asset stripping on the way.

There was a time when stock photography made the photographer and the agency good money. It was a symbiotic relationship: the more commercial your images, the more you made, and the more valuable you were to the agency. Top stock photographers were rock stars, and the release of a new stock catalogue had all the pizzazz of a Hollywood Blockbuster (for me, at least). I remember at college in the 1980s, one such stock photography A-lister gave a talk about the money he was making with the legendary stock agency Tony Stone, and how, as long as we shot on fixed lenses (no zooms allowed) and used transparency film, we could share in his success.

I even recall how the auditorium gasped when the strange grey breezeblock-shaped briefcase next to him started ringing. A mobile telephone! He took the call in front of a hall full of awestruck photography students. We were sold. 

The inevitable downfall of a giant

For a while, it seemed there was enough for everyone, but that wasn’t enough for some, and that symbiotic relationship became cancerous. Those monthly stock agency receipt notices became smaller and smaller. The only option was to submit more and more images for less and less money. The laws of scale may have worked in Getty’s favour, but they were economic ruin for photographers.

Thus Getty disrupted and destroyed photographic markets in its vision for infinite growth; in doing so, it conditioned buyers to expect vast quantities of imagery for less money. The maths still worked for them, provided it continued to grow; for the rest of the market, it salted the well.

Getty swallowed competitors until few remained. Once-grand names are now mere footnotes in  photographic history: Telegraph Colour Library, Allsport, Colourific! 

Then AI arrived and scuppered Getty’s plans. How about all the images you can imagine – for the price of one teeny-tiny monthly fee? No matter how fine your fare, if someone opens a stall next door, giving away something very similar, you will eventually go out of business. There was no loyalty left on Fleet Street. And few people were willing to pay for excellence when ‘good enough’ is part of a free buffet. AI has made everyone experts in mediocrity. 

Getty’s response was to bet the farm on a merger with the giant agency Shutterstock. More growth! But that plan failed – Getty walked away from the deal when the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) insisted Shutterstock first sell off its global editorial business including Shutterstock Editorial, Backgrid and Splash. Getty’s fate was sealed.

No one saw it coming; they never do. New technology always disrupts in ways we can’t quite imagine. Think what would happen to Amazon if you could 3D print everything from grommets to ballpoint pens at home for free. Its business model would vanish just like Getty’s.

Getty was a bright star that grew too big too quickly and then imploded, leaving a black hole that sucked editorial photography into oblivion with it. I would say ‘I told you so’ but what’s the point when there’s no one left to listen?

Everyone’s been to the Highlands, so minimise travel and visit the spectacular Scottish Lowlands for your next Scotland trip, by Alexandra Pereira

The first thing I notice at Glenapp Castle are the curling stones. Wedging open the heavy doors, these granite boulders are hewn from Ailsa Craig, the island you can see from the windows of this mighty Scottish property.

Inside, every corridor gives period drama; every staircase evokes a mysterious aristocrat descending at midnight.

This is The Wicker Man country, where remote islands, peculiar local traditions and mist-shrouded seas lend themselves to cinematic drama. The 1973 cult classic, starring Edward Woodward and Christopher Lee, was filmed around these stretches of south-west Scotland. Thankfully, our own story is more relaxing.

Scotland’s luxury travel industry places so much emphasis on the Highlands. But Glenapp, a Relais & Châteaux hotel near Ballantrae, makes a compelling case for staying in the Scottish Lowlands. Take a scenic train up through the Lakes from Euston to Glasgow (3.5h) and arrange a Glenapp transfer (90min).

The Scottish Lowlands

Set in 36 acres of gardens and woodland, the 21-bedroom castle looks across the Irish Sea towards the 99 hectares-wide Ailsa Craig and the Mull of Kintyre. Roe deer move through the grounds, woodpeckers provide the soundtrack, and the staff are warm rather than starchy. This feels like a house with real history, rather than a hotel striving to manufacture one.

My dear friend Will – my top companion for rogue country rambles, and my trusty deliverer of room service in robes – is a television producer with an eye for a location. We’ve been here five minutes and he’s already mentally casting this place.

Scotland holidays: windows frame Ailsa Craig

I’m staying in The Nest, a one-bedroom cottage suite in the estate’s 1830s walled garden. Converted from a former tearoom, this property, which launched in the summer, offers 60 square metres of period antiques, rich fabrics, a log burner and woodland views. In the garden I spot frogs and dragonflies. Outdoors, a private sauna, ice plunge tub and shower are hidden by hedgerow, and beyond, there are magnificent grounds.

The gardens benefit from the region’s mild microclimate, influenced by the Gulf Stream. Three botanical gardens in the wider area, including Logan Botanic Garden, testify to the conditions that allow plants to flourish here despite Scotland’s northerly latitude. Snow is less of a fixture, making getting here a safe bet unlike some of Scotland’s more northerly castles.

Dinner begins with cocktails in the drawing room, where ceiling-high windows frame Ailsa Craig. An optical illusion gives the impression the island is close, but it is actually ten miles from the mainland. Will is still scouting locations while I’m more interested in what’s being poured.

Scrambles to the black, glossy waters

Executive chef Peter Howarth and his team serve a seven-course tasting menu, with a three-course alternative. Highlights included fat scallops, earthy potatoes, wonderful rhubarb dessert. Extra points for the silver service, which justifies itself in these surroundings, and chats with staff in the candlelit dining room.

The restaurant holds three AA Rosettes, and its kitchen draws on the estate’s garden, polytunnels and 150-foot glasshouse. A wine flight is a worthwhile indulgence; as is a dram from the castle’s single-malt range afterwards. For lunch or dinner, The Azalea, housed in the Victorian glasshouse, offers a relaxed alternative.

Paths go through woodland and down into the glen towards the coast. We enjoy multiple scrambles down to the black, glossy waters under the shadows of the firs, enjoying that the only sounds are of the water and the snaps of twigs.

The Scottish Lowlands’ epic Galloway Hills complete the view on clear days. The weather supplies its own filmset values: shafts of sunlight, sudden rain and skies that change mood between footsteps. I remain forever and newly enchanted by these lands and the way light falls, reminding me of Scandinavia where I once lived.

Birds make a racket

Eventually, the island demands more than a supporting role. We head out to sea. Ailsa Craig rises from the Firth of Clyde nine miles offshore, its granite prized by sporting curlers for around 250 years. An estimated 60 to 70 per cent of the world’s curling stones are still made from it, including those used at every Winter Olympics since 2006.

Perhaps the strangest team sport, athletes play a sort of chess-on-ice, sliding granite rocks towards targets. The stone is carefully prised from the land in 20-tonne chunks, before a laborious sculpting and sanding down to begin fashioning these obscure, elegant instruments.

Tens of thousands of gannets crowd the island’s cliffs alongside guillemots, razorbills and kittiwakes. They make an absolute racket as we near, the waves bouncing our boat around.

Rats introduced in the 19th century devastated eggs and chicks, and puffins disappeared as breeding birds. Following an eradication campaign in 1991, puffins returned to breed in 2002.

Watching the birds wheel above the cliffs, I grasp the region’s cinematic appeal. My bird-lover pal Will grips his binoculars ever tighter as more and more come, his elbows doing laps of the horizon as he moves them backwards and forwards.

Piles of lobster and mackerel

We are cold and ready for that next dram, and a spot of lunch. Back on the mainland, we drive south to Portpatrick, near Scotland’s southernmost tip, where the harbour occupies a natural amphitheatre in the coast. Personal drivers can be arranged with Glenapp should you be carless, and these trips are especially welcome on bad weather days when the boat can’t go out.

In this tiny, hilly town, a giant anchor and a gate opening towards the sea tell the story of this place, shaped by its relationship with the water. Steps, like those of an amphitheatre, lead to the sea, and in the distance we just about make out Belfast.

It’s a Tuesday afternoon, but the Crown Hotel is busy. It’s a harbour-front homely pub with laminated menus and a lively, welcoming vibe. Winner of the AA Seafood Pub of Scotland award, the area is increasingly championed for oysters. We study laminated menus and end up with piles of fresh local fish and shellfish: half a lobster and mackerel, with salads and cobs.

The Highlands will always have drama

Along this same short part of coastline, some 22km from Portpatrick, Cairnryan’s Stena Line ferries connect Scotland with Northern Ireland. Tourism in this corner of Ayrshire isn’t fully realised. The campaign for a Galloway National Park reflects the desire to give this landscape greater recognition, which will help the local economy.

As for the locals, pride extends to the produce. One claim I hear is that Galloway has the best milk in Scotland, thanks to its grass, sea air and mineral-rich soils, the humble brag capturing the region’s confidence in its produce.

At nearby Bladnoch Distillery – a 40 minute drive from Portpatrick – the connection between landscape and spirit is summed up in one memorable phrase: “Today’s rain is tomorrow’s whisky.” I don’t visit this time round, but our driver has samples, and this wisdom to share, and we order another dram back at the Castle after being pelted with rain on another glen amble.

The Highlands will always have drama but Ayrshire and Galloway offer something more understated. For a cinematic year-round weekend escape, it’s every bit as compelling and cosy.

Book this Scotland holiday

Glenapp Castle’s Garden View Suites start from £595 per night. The Nest B&B rates start from £837.25 per night in low season, rising to £1,575 per night in peak season. The Ailsa Craig Boat Trip is £1,250 for a half-day experience. British banks are becoming increasingly reliant on a handful of foreign tech giants to power their AI ambitions, new research from Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority has revealed, raising concerns over the City’s dependence on overseas infrastructure.

The three largest cloud computing providers account for 79 per cent of reported supplier relationships among financial services firms, according to a joint survey by the Bank and Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).

More than a third of cloud relationships were deemed critical to operations and difficult to replace, yet just 35 per cent of those had tested plans to switch providers in the event of disruption.

The findings come amid growing scrutiny of Britain’s reliance on US technology companies, with a recent Google Cloud outage highlighting the potential consequences of disruption to infrastructure used by banks and other businesses.

The Treasury Committee has pressed regulators over their oversight of major cloud providers, warning that an outage could have serious consequences for financial stability.

Meanwhile, the report found that third-party providers account for 53 per cent of systems considered highly material to their operations. However, just 24 per cent of respondents reported having deep knowledge of their most important third-party AI systems, with 81 per cent instead relying on assurances from suppliers and contractual protections.

“Nearly all firms have an AI policy in place, however very few have a clear understanding of the third-party AI systems they are using”, said Sebastien Marchon, chief executive of fintech firm Rydoo. “That needs to change if firms want to fully leverage the benefits and ensure they can answer to regulators”.

Marchon said newer integration technologies, including Model Context Protocols, could help businesses connect AI tools to their existing software, but warned that oversight of external providers needed to improve.

Tempered AI ambitions

A separate KPMG survey found that 87 per cent of UK financial services leaders believe AI will have a greater impact on the industry than the 1986 Big Bang reforms, which transformed London’s financial markets.

But the bank’s research suggests that firms face significant obstacles in putting the technology to work. Almost a quarter cited difficulties integrating AI into existing business processes as a major barrier, while 22 per cent pointed to outdated systems and infrastructure.

The FCA last week warned that some financial firms were deploying AI without adequate governance or human oversight, urging businesses to make sure senior managers remained accountable for the technology.

John Healey will set his fiscal headroom at a minimum of £15bn, City analysts have predicted, although closer attention will be paid to the Chancellor’s spending restraint. 

Economists at major banks are anticipating Healey’s buffer against the main fiscal rule to shrink slightly. The borrowing rule states that day-to-day government spending should at least match projected tax receipts by 2030.

Top economists have said the Office for Budget Responsibility, the independent forecaster whose calculations determine whether the Chancellor has a grip over public finances, will list a number of costs from higher borrowing in part due to the Iran war. 

At this year’s Spring Statement, former Chancellor Rachel Reeves’ buffer stood at £23.6bn, although the estimate was calculated before the US and Israel launched strikes in Iran, which led to significant trade disruption of oil and gas across the Gulf region. 

While higher earnings forecasts and extra income from the energy profit levy and general taxation could drive receipts, the heavy costs from higher debt interest payments, spending commitments on defence and rising inflation means Healey is heading into the Budget with the headroom standing at closer to £10bn, according to Deutsche Bank and UBS. 

Healey’s headroom ‘less of a focus’

Researchers at Deutsche Bank said a collection of taxes on online retailers, gambling, banking profits and narrowing the tax gap means Healey is set for tax rises worth around £5bn at the Budget. 

“Modest tax rises and efficiency savings, we think, will bring the Chancellor’s primary headroom to £15.7bn,” the bank’s UK economist Sanjay Raja said. 

However, he added that markets would view Budget measures cautiously as they wait for further announcements on defence spending and departmental cuts over the next year. The government is tasked with spending about £11bn more each year if it wishes to lift military funding to three per cent of GDP by 2030, while higher inflation is expected to weaken the value of public expenditure. 

“While the public finances will have taken a modest hit relative to the Spring Statement, markets will be less focused on the headline measures announced on Budget Day and more focused on what they signal about the road ahead,” Raja noted.

“Put simply, can the Chancellor provide households and businesses with some breathing space today, while convincing investors that the much bigger spending decisions that loom next year will be funded responsibly?” 

Healey is also expected to announce temporary measures on the cost of living, including extending a freeze on fuel duty, providing a warm homes discount to millions of households and offering businesses some support with costs on employment and energy. 

Morgan Stanley’s UK economist Bruna Skarica said the headroom figure would be “less of a focus” for the bond markets as investors “zoomed in more on the perceived plausibility of the fiscal plan and any near-term borrowing increases which might be presented as one-offs and temporary, but seen by the market as permanent”. 

Pantheon Macroeconomics analysts Rob Wood and Elliott Jordan-Doak told market clients in a note that “less headroom and kicking tough decisions on defence and other spending into the long grass” could push up gilt yields after the fiscal statement. 

“Avoiding addressing known spending pressures now undercuts the credibility of planned fiscal consolidation,” they said.

“Markets would need to believe that a government politically unwilling, or unable, to tighten now could deliver even larger consolidation immediately before an election.”

Rugby union and league are growing in the Indo-Pacific, as is the investment from central governments of dominant regional powers. Matt Hardy asks why.

Amid the disruption at airports in Saudi Arabia, the limited access through the Strait of Hormuz and the nagging feeling that the world is on the verge of doom, soft power feels increasingly important. But no longer do quiet meetings always take place in the corners of a consulate or mid-way through a state dinner; instead, new ways to influence geopolitics and exert control are being developed – and one of those is sport.

Recent events have shown how football’s geography is so important to its politics – and who stays in the top job – and it is no different when assessing how both rugby league and union are being used in a wider game of battleships within the Indo-Pacific region and beyond. 

Take the Australian government, which has been an underwriter of the Papua New Guinea rugby league entry into the NRL. The PNG Chiefs – interestingly, sponsored by ExxonMobil branch PNG LMG – forms a key cog in a £300m plan by Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to keep the island nation within the political sphere of its southern neighbour. 

With three Rugby World Cups – spanning union and league – in four years, Australia is also backing Fiji, Samoa, Tonga through rugby development, while it had involvement in the recent Super Rugby franchise expansion.

Soft power playing part

But why? Because of China and wider actors, of course. China’s Belt and Road initiative is usually associated with Africa but it extends into the Pacific, too. The nation built the Pacific Games Stadium Complex on the Solomon Islands, did similar in Fiji and Samoa, and donated to the Fijian women’s rugby union team last year to celebrate International Women’s Day.

“The South-West Pacific region, sometimes known as Melanesia, is one of the world’s most strategically important trade chokepoints and is therefore an increasingly sensitive territory,” sport and geopolitics scholar Professor Simon Chadwick tells City AM. “It is a maritime gateway that forms a vital part of what is often referred to as the Second Island Chain, making it a crucial buffer zone for Australia’s northern approaches.

“A range of diplomatic instruments is being deployed by these countries which extends to the use of sport. In particular, both countries have been investing in the Melanesian game, indeed interventions by the Australian government now see teams from Papua New Guinea competing in both its union and league competitions.”

But the two main players aren’t the only ones on the pitch. Qatar offered subsidies to the Pacific Islands if it won the right to stage a Rugby World Cup, while also being part of an agreement with the French Rugby Union – alongside China – to develop programmes across the game.

A political pawn

France itself funds rugby programmes in New Caledonia and Wallis and Futuna and has coaching agreements with Fiji, Samoa and Tonga. Japan does similar, while the UK uses the Ministry of Defence and rugby to build relations. The US and UAE also use sports envoy programmes to further their cause.

This helps to explain a potential new NRL franchise partly based in and backed by New Zealand, with home games taking place in the Cook Islands, United States, Tonga and Samoa – the latter is currently seeing government threats to its rugby union programme. And to top it all off, next year’s rugby union World Cup will feature Hong Kong for the first time, except in 2027 they’ll play as Hong Kong China.

“The region is rich in deposits of gold, copper, nickel and liquified natural gas,” Chadwick added. “All of which makes the region a key area for power projection by the likes of Australia and China, which compete for power and influence there. 

“Sport clearly and increasingly plays a crucial role in building relations, extending influence and projecting soft power.”

Investing in sport is always a popular vote winner at home, but internationally it is a crucial part of developing relationships with new friends, or shoring up backing against political enemies. Who said sport and politics aren’t intertwined?

Children may be being given SpaceX shares over in the States, but UK pension reforms means Brits can access superstar companies through their savings, writes Ian Cornelius

News arrived last week that Elon Musk will give every American child a share in SpaceX. It comes days after Anthropic, the frontier AI firm, announced plans for five per cent of its shares to be placed in a ‘public benefit’ fund. OpenAI, its competitor, reportedly floated a similar proposal in July.

Whatever you might think about the necessity or underlying motivations of these plans, it’s worth pausing on why they’re so eye-catching in today’s market.

Consider this: When Microsoft listed in 1986, it was worth less than a billion dollars. Anyone with a modest shareholding came along for the extraordinary ride that followed. You could say it grew ‘in public’.

By contrast, early growth in today’s superstar companies is the reserve of billionaires, sovereign wealth funds, various endowments and the sort of global-scale pension funds that historically the UK has largely lacked. Today’s Microsofts can stay private for a lot longer. The value that these companies reach over a handful of years has already been captured, to the benefit of wealthy early investors. This means that, for the most part, ordinary British savers are left out.

In this era of dominant private markets, UK pension funds must find a way for British workers and savers to access the widest possible range of investments. That might be the chance of catching the next superstar, or diversifying market risk through ‘boring’ but stable assets like housing and infrastructure. This is how the richest ensure their wealth increases no matter what: they combine a strategy of ‘limited downside/unlimited upside’ with stable income regardless of what goes on in public markets. The same approach should be available to everyone, but it gets harder as so much value is kept behind closed doors.

How pension reforms are helping Brits

This week, the ABI published the latest figures on progress towards the pension industry’s Mansion House commitments. Signatories committed 10 per cent of their portfolios to be invested in private markets, half of which will be invested in the UK. The figures from the ABI show it is possible: more than £11bn has been invested so far in UK private markets, giving pension fund members access to what is otherwise off-limits.

For example, Nest, where I work, is an investor in the British startup Wayve, which is bringing its self-driving cars to London, one of the world’s first cities to host the new tech. 

We’re also in on companies like Citation, a tech firm in the North West providing compliance services to 110,000 customers, and 9fin, a British fintech startup valued at $1.3bn. In total, we have committed £3bn to unlisted equities – around five per cent of our portfolio – one in every five pounds of which is invested in the UK.

All three are examples of the UK’s world-class tech ecosystem, and they sit alongside other great firms, homes and infrastructure in Britain and beyond whose returns our members might never access without the reach that their pension fund provides.

I’m especially proud of the fact that our scale has enabled us to do this on our terms: we do not pay performance fees – all of the upside goes to our members. Investing on their own terms is another thing that the wealthy get access to, but that we now offer to savers by merit of our scale, positioning and thoughtful approach.

But what matters to pension funds like us is the new opportunity and unique access it gives to our members. They won’t have to wait for a billionaire to give away shares in Wayve and 9fin and Citation, or in thousands of others like them – they’re already bought in.

Ian Cornelius is CEO of Nest Pensions

Despite the professional services sector dodging tax hikes on LLPs in last year’s Budget, it remains unclear whether Chancellor John Healey will impose tax changes this time round, but Rosie Harris-Davison writes that experts have warned against any tax burdens on the sector.

In the lead-up to last year’s Budget, whispers circulated for weeks that Rachel Reeves was considering taxing LLP firms. However, after sector-wide lobbying against the move, the former Chancellor rolled back the plans.

The LLP model came into force over 25 years ago and is used by many firms across the professional services industry, including law firms, accountancy firms, and some doctors. It is a structure in which members, known as partners, invest their own capital, take on the risk, and, in return, do not pay corporate tax on their profits.

Private client tax partner at RSM, Chris Etherington, told City AM that if tax hikes are imposed on LLPs in the upcoming Budget, it “would lead to some competition issues” among firms and disruption to the wider LLP market.

“You’ve got some large law firms which are not set up as LLPs are just general partnerships. If you’re taxing one more, you’re distorting the market slightly,” Etherington said. He added that the move risks the market becoming more disrupted as firms “could just move offshore, frankly.”

In terms of the impact of LLP tax hikes on the firms’ equity partners, Etherington said it “will have a similar impact to a rising corporation tax”, but it will be equivalent to income tax hitting their personal taxes, and have “a knock-on effect potentially” for customers, employees, and business investment.

While risking their own capital and not benefiting from the protections available to employees at LLPs, partners already face tax rates close to 50 per cent, meaning they will bear a heavy brunt of any tax on the firms.

The professional and business services sector is an economic engine for Britain, and in 2025, it contributed £335bn to the UK economy and is one of the UK’s largest employers.

Sean Drury, Head of tax at Blick Rothenberg, told City AM the government “should be wary” of imposing tax on LLPs as the partnership structure “has been effective in attracting professional and financial services organisations to the UK.”

“Similar structures are available elsewhere, so I am unsure that the government is looking for an outcome which would disincentivise organisations to base or invest in the UK where they have other locations for the investment,” Drury said.

Budget may have tweaks rather than shocks

Alexandra Ueno-Park, partner at Haynes Boone, told City AM that despite nothing being confirmed yet in the upcoming Budget, she expects it to “bring tweaks rather than shocks”, but firms would “be wise to model the potential cost now.”

Back in July, the Supreme Court reignited anxieties over possible tax hikes for LLPs after billionaire and founder of hedge fund, BlueCrest Capital Management, Michael Platt, lost a £200m tax battle with HMRC after the court rejected the firm’s argument that its partners were technically self-employed and therefore not subject to the same income tax and national insurance as normal employees.

“After years of upheaval over salaried member rules, Supreme Court litigation and carried interest reforms, professional services need one thing above all: stability. If change is coming, it should come only after a full and proper consultation,” Ueno-Park said.

Sarah Curzon, tax partner at MHA, told City AM any tax changes to the LLP model “could have significant consequences for the UK professional services sector.”

“Professional services is an important UK growth sector and one in which the UK has a strong international position,” Curzon said. “With employment costs having increased and firms also needing to make substantial investment in technology, data and AI, further increases in the tax cost of operating an LLP could add to those pressures.”

Curzon added that if any tax changes “significantly alter the relative tax position of LLPs”, she anticipates that firms will “review whether the LLP remains the most appropriate structure.”

Legal sector sounds alarm

Last year, the legal sector sounded the alarm over Reeves’ proposal, with industry bodies such as the Law Society demanding “absolute clarity” that the plans had been quashed.

Colin Passmore, Chairman of the City of London Law Society (CLLS), echoed the same concerns ahead of this year’s Budget.

“Any return of last year’s proposals to extend national insurance to LLP partners would be both unfair and damaging to growth. LLPs are taxed in the same way as other partnerships, so there is no loophole to close,” Passmore told City AM.

Passmore said any changes would “create new distortions rather than correct an existing one.”

“Those distortions would push firms to restructure how they pay and organise their partners, or to move work to competing centres such as New York, Singapore and the Gulf,” Passmore said.

“That would undermine one of the UK’s most successful exports at precisely the moment the government is looking to the private sector for growth. We fully support a fair tax system, which is why a change of this significance should only follow proper consultation with the profession,” he added.

When approached for a comment, a Treasury spokesperson said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the Chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

To achieve sustainable economic growth, the government must move beyond short-term Budget fixes and provide businesses with long-term certainty through tax stability and regulatory reform, says Alan Vallance

“You can’t invest what you don’t have or when you are unsure what extra tax or regulatory burden is around the corner.” 

That was how one of our members summed up what businesses need from the Chancellor’s forthcoming Budget. It captures something I hear repeatedly from business leaders: the frustration of being asked to deliver growth, while facing rising costs, higher taxes and growing regulatory demands. 

The scale of that pressure is clear in our latest Business Confidence Monitor. Business confidence has now been negative for seven consecutive quarters, matching the longest uninterrupted period since the global financial crisis. For many businesses, that means postponing investment, putting recruitment on hold and diverting resources away from growth simply to absorb rising costs. 

I recognise the difficult choices facing the Chancellor, but when the public finances are under pressure, we cannot afford to see businesses simply as another source of revenue. They are also the engine of the growth on which those revenues depend. 

As finance leaders, business owners and trusted advisers, our members see these pressures first-hand across the country. In our polling ahead of the Budget, more than two-thirds of respondents said greater certainty over tax and business regulation would make them or their clients more likely to invest over the next three years. 

Give businesses breathing space

That should give the Chancellor pause for thought. Policies that discourage investment and hiring risk making his fiscal challenge harder, not easier. This Budget is an opportunity to stop adding to those pressures and give businesses the breathing space they need to grow. 

The Chancellor should start by ruling out further increases in employment taxes during this Parliament and freezing the business rates multiplier for 2027/28, while committing to wider reform of a system that too often penalises expansion. 

Reducing costs is only part of the answer. Businesses also need confidence that the economic and tax environment will remain stable enough for them to plan ahead. Greater clarity over the government’s fiscal rules, including what constitutes “current budget balance”, would help avoid unwelcome surprises for markets. There is also much the government could do to make running a business easier. Improving HMRC’s performance would reduce the delays and unnecessary costs businesses face, while expanding the Growth Guarantee Scheme would help smaller firms access the finance they need to invest and grow. 

None of this requires the Chancellor to abandon fiscal discipline. It means recognising that stronger businesses and healthier public finances go hand in hand. Yet the problems facing British business cannot be solved through one Budget alone. Britain’s increasingly complex tax system is already holding back growth and risks becoming unfit for the economy of the future without fundamental reform. 

Successive Budgets have added rules, thresholds and reliefs, often without enough consideration of how they fit together. The result is one of the world’s most complex tax codes, one that has grown more than fourteenfold over the past 50 years.  

At the same time, the economy our tax system needs to support is changing rapidly. AI, shifting demographics and weak productivity growth raise difficult questions about where future tax revenues will come from and how we fund public services. 

We cannot assume that a tax system built up through decades of piecemeal changes will be fit for an economy undergoing profound transformation. That is why we have established the Future of Tax Commission, an independent body chaired by former Treasury Minister Mark Hoban which begins its two-year programme of work in January 2027, to examine what a better tax system should look like and how we might get there. 

This Budget can give businesses room to breathe. But securing Britain’s long-term prosperity means looking beyond individual Budgets and asking how our tax system can better support growth and sustainable public finances. At ICAEW, we have begun that work. I want government, businesses and policymakers to be part of it. We have an opportunity to think seriously about the tax system Britain will need in the decades ahead, and we should not waste it.

Alan Vallance is chief executive at ICAEW

The watchdog has fined HW Fisher LLP and one of its partners £200,000 for serious professional failures during an audit of Liberty Commodities, a group within metals tycoon Sanjeev Gupta’s GFG Alliance.

The Financial Reporting Council (FRC) said HW Fisher LLP and lead auditor Simon Mott-Cowan showed a pervasive lack of “professional scepticism” during the audit for the financial year ended 31 March 2020. The regulator identified serious breaches across seven key audit areas, including revenue recognition, debt recoverability and going concern assessments.

The regulator also said the firm failed to properly understand Liberty Commodities’s business model. Most of Liberty Commodities’s sales were ‘back-to-back’, meaning it would purchase materials from a supplier only after agreeing to sell the same goods onward to a customer. The business model relied heavily on supply chain finance facilities from scandal-hit Greensill Capital UK and Wyelands Bank to finance commodity trading transactions.

Wyelands was also part of the GFG Alliance. In March 2025, PwC was fined over £4.5m for its audits of Wyelands Bank.

Greensill Capital, exposed through its ties to Gupta’s GFG Alliance, collapsed in 2021, triggering a major financial and political scandal. The UK Insolvency Service banned the founder, Lex Greensill, in June from serving as a company director for nine years.

Andrew Twomey, FRC, acting deputy executive counsel, said: “HW Fisher and Mr Mott-Cowan failed to comprehend and respond appropriately to obvious risks, including the risk of withdrawal of the Greensill financing facilities, despite the growing public scrutiny, as reported in the media at the time of the audit, on Greensill’s exposure to the GFG Alliance.”

“The case highlights, in particular, the importance of auditors’ work in understanding the entity and its environment, and how failures in this area can undermine the ultimate performance of the audit as a whole,” he added.

The FRC opened the probe in February 2022. On Tuesday, the regulator fined HW Fisher £200,000, reduced to £140,000 on admission, and formally declared that it failed to meet the requirements. The regulator fined Mott-Cowan £25,000, reduced to £17,500, and formally declared he failed to meet the requirements. The FRC said that, during its investigation, he voluntarily retired from all audit work at the end of 2025.

Private equity powers Sumer’s expansion

London-based accountancy firm HW Fisher merged with Sumer in October 2024 but retained its independent brand name. The FRC sanctions against HW Fisher predate its merger with the accountancy firm.

Former KPMG chief operating officer Warren Mead founded the fast-growing accountancy firm Sumer to serve the SME market.

The company, now the UK’s twelfth-largest accountancy group, is owned by private equity firm Penta Capital Partners. Last week, US investment firm TPG agreed to lead an investment backing Sumer at a valuation exceeding £1bn.

City grandees have called on the government to revive “animal spirits” in London’s capital markets and accelerate regulatory reform on the anniversary of the Big Bang.

Industry leaders told City AM the City has enjoyed decades of success since the sweeping deregulation of the Square Mile in 1986 but Britain’s financial services industry is now facing existential threats in the form of a downturn in public equity investment and a flight of firms away from the London Stock Exchange.

“No international financial center has a God-given right to success, and complacency is the single most dangerous thing that any international financial centre can indulge,” Miles Celic, chief executive of TheCityUK, told City AM.

He added the Big Bang does not need to be “followed by a Big Bang 2.0 and then in another 40 years a Big Bang 3.0” and reform of the UK’s capital market should instead be viewed as “a journey”.

Spearheaded by Margaret Thatcher’s government on October 27 1986, the Big Bang dismantled fixed commissions, ended the divide between brokers and jobbers, and opened London’s trading floors to foreign banks and screen-based electronic dealing.

Since taking power in 2024, Labour has promised to reinvigorate the City through scrapping burdensome regulation. Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves handed watchdogs a secondary growth objective that required them to consider the international competitiveness of the UK alongside their core roles of stability. 

“Regulators have done a lot to improve the environment and improve the opportunity for companies to list in the UK,” Steven Fine, chief executive of Peel Hunt, said. 

“What we need now is a big bang on the capital side to reignite the City’s animal spirits. We need to incentivise domestic investors to back UK listed stocks and to stop rewarding them for investing overseas.”

Stacey Parsons, managing director at Retail Book, said: “The piece of the puzzle that’s now needed is confidence and stability. Less policy and more practice. We need to start treating UK capital markets as national infrastructure.” 

The London Stock Exchange has faced a testing few years with a drought of new IPOs and a flurry of delistings and foreign takeovers. Since the start of 2023 there have been 166 bids for firms with a price tag over £100m with the collective value topping £180bn. This is compared to just 11 IPOs above £100m for a total value of £6bn.

“Forty years on from the Big Bang, the London Stock Exchange continues to evolve, but our purpose remains the same: supporting ambitious companies and the investors who back them,” Julia Hoggett, chief executive of the London Stock Exchange, said.

“That continuous innovation is vital to ensuring that our markets are able to unlock the capital that delivers what matters – investment in businesses, jobs and growth across the country.”

In the 2025 Budget, Reeves launched a stamp duty holiday, removing the 0.5 per cent levy on UK stocks for newly-listed companies in their first three years of trading. But industry has continued to urge the government to go further and boost tax incentives to invest. 

Their warnings come ahead of a John Healey’s maiden Budget on Wednesday in which he is expected to hit the UK’s banking sector with higher taxes. He has reportedly ruled out hiking capital gains tax over fears it would hammer investment into the UK.

“[The Big Bang] made the UK internationally competitive and unleashed our country’s animal spirits in the decades that followed,” shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith told City AM. “In the week of the Budget, Chancellor Healey must remember that when the City wins, so does Britain,” he added.

The FTSE 100 bank’s stock slid seven per cent in early trading to 1,269.0p in a move that shed around £16bn from the firm’s market capitalisation. It also put it on track to lose its crown as the City’s biggest listed firm on valuation.

It comes despite the bank revealing plans to return $1bn to shareholders through a buyback programme after it scored a $9.63bn profit for the quarter. This was broadly in line with the consensus expectations of $9.69bn.

But revenue missed the mark after HSBC reported $18.6bn for the period, below the forecast of $18.9bn. The over $300m miss followed underperformance in banking net interest income, which delivered about $11.6bn, some $247m below expectations.

Revenue in the bank’s wealth division was also softer than expected at $2.7bn, compared to a $2.8bn consensus.

“The numbers themselves are not disastrous,” Will Howlett, financials analyst at Quilter Cheviot, said.

“The issue is that HSBC has set a high bar for itself. Following a strong run for the shares, investors have become accustomed to robust results, so even relatively modest misses can prompt a sharper reaction. Today’s fall therefore looks more like disappointment against high expectations than a significant deterioration in the underlying business.”

The firm also revealed an interim dividend of $0.1 per ordinary share, which equates to around $1.7bn being dished out to investors. Along with the buyback, this could bring returns for the quarter to around $2.7bn.

“Our performance shows that in a more complex world clients continue to turn to us to navigate uncertainty and seize new opportunities. It also reflects consistent execution of our strategic priorities with pace, precision and discipline,” Georges Elhedery, group chief executive, said.

“As we simplify HSBC, we are creating greater capacity to invest, grow and deliver strong returns for our shareholders.”

Operating expenses at the bank dropped 12 per cent to $8.8bn, mainly due to the absence of a major legal charge that dragged up the previous year’s figure.

HSBC made a $1.1b provision in its third quarter results in 2025 following a Luxembourg court rejecting the bank’s appeal in regards to an investment fraud case associated with the Bernie Madoff scandal.

The legal claims against the bank revolved around allegations that it breached its supervisory duties by failing to properly safeguard or verify the existence of the assets and thereby facilitating the continuation of the fraud.

Just over a year ago, the bank also revealed plans to buy out minority shareholders in Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Bank.     Having shaken off early legal threats from PwC, secured 120 clients, and already won work from traditional rivals, two former Big Four heavyweights told Rosie Harris-Davison that their advisory firm, Unity Advisory, is not a challenger but a contender in the evolving market.

    Marissa Thomas, former chief operating officer and managing partner at PwC UK for 32 years until 2025, and Steve Varley, former chairman and managing partner of EY UK and Ireland, founded the private-equity-backed firm Unity Advisory to “modernise” the advisory model.

    “I had strongly held views on how advisory needed to be different, by putting talent and expertise at the heart of the model, and leveraging technology and AI responsibly to accelerate delivery,” Thomas told City AM. “I just wanted to be part of creating something that was the next chapter versus trying to update something that needs retrofitting.”

    Since Unity Advisory took on its first client in November last year, after two Big Four veterans founded it in April, the advisory firm now has 120 clients on its books, serving primarily private-equity-backed businesses and private equity firms, alongside some listed companies, and shows no signs of slowing down.

    “We’re not a challenger, we are a contender,” Thomas said, adding that the firm is “winning work from a broad range of competitors”.

    However, the firm’s early journey hit some bumps after its debut when reports said PwC sent legal threats in February to senior members of the advisory firm who had jumped ship from the Big Four giant. But months later, the heat seems to have cooled, as Thomas told City AM that there is “no ongoing litigation or legal battle with PwC, or any of the Big Four [firms].”

    “I’d say the relationships are appropriately cordial,” Thomas added.

    Firm targets outcome-based billing

    Varley said after he left EY, his previous clients asked what he was doing next, and when he shared the idea of Unity Advisory, his former clients were “really interested in continuing a relationship”, as he stated with an advisory firm that focused on “outcomes” instead of the traditional advisory model of billing by the hour, which “got him thinking” even more about the business idea.

    He said the firm is now “a viable alternative” to the Big Four and other mid-market advisory firms, and compares its conflict-free business model to being “like a speedboat rather than an oil tanker”, able to move faster and adapt quicker than large, well-established legacy firms.

    The Mayfair-headquartered firm uses AI and proprietary software to increase client-facing time and reduce administrative work, which Varley said makes Unity an “AI-powered” firm, enabling it to speed up delivery while retaining human judgement. “We want to work out the value we’re going to create together, and then we’d rather be paid on the value creation rather than the billable hours,” he said.

    This comes as the Big Four and the wider professional services sector increasingly invest in stronger ‘human skills’ as AI reshapes the industry.

    PE backer expectations ‘exceeded’

    Unity Advisory signed a deal with US private equity backer Warburg Pincus for up to $300m (£224.8m) in funding last April.

    “We’ve got a growing book of business locally, a lot of clients that love our model and want something different, and we’ve got some very, very talented people that have joined us. It’s a really good market for professional services talent,” she added.
