]]>

A MINI autonomously rolls off a U.K. production line using Embotech technology. Source: BMW Group

As vehicles come off the production line, human drivers typically need to get into each one to drive them to be parked or loaded onto trucks. Embotech and BMW today said they have moved 1 million vehicles using Embotech’s automated driving technology across four sites in the U.K. and Germany.

“Automated vehicle movements only create value when intelligence, safety, and reliability come together,” stated Andreas Kyrtatos, CEO of Embotech. “This milestone shows what is possible when proven technology is integrated into live production and operated reliably around the clock.”

Spun out of ETH Zurich in 2013, Embotech claimed that it is a global leader in safety-certified SAE Level 4 autonomous driving systems for industrial logistics and the first company worldwide to hold multiple TÜV-certified Level 4 solutions. Its two certified systems – Automated Vehicle Marshalling (AVM) and Autonomous Tractor Solution (ATS) – are built on a shared platform and are deployed in automotive factories, vehicle distribution centers, ports, and logistics yards.

The Zurich-based company said its technology can improve safety, productivity, resilience, and sustainability across logistics operations. In July, Embotech entered a strategic partnership with HTEC to scale deployment of autonomous driving across vehicles, customer programs, and industrial sites.

Submit your innovation now!

Embotech helps automaker increase flexibility

While automotive OEMs are already major users of industrial automation, they are continuing to digitize and adopt new technologies to make production processes more efficient, noted Embotech. However, much of the market remains at the pilot stage, autonomously operating only a limited number of vehicles, it said.

The Automated Driving In-Plant is vehicle- and OEM-agnostic and connects to existing drive-by-wire capabilities.

“Perception for [AVM] is in the infrastructure — vehicles don’t need self-driving capabilities or extra sensors,” Eva Beck, chief commercial officer at Embotech, told The Robot Report. “Hesai lidars are mounted in the production environment, so there are no hardware modifications. In the factory, we have a standardized software interface, offboard computers, and servers that optimize driving trajectories 10 times per second.”

Embotech provides key components, including its AI-based software for perception, prediction, and planning, which enables vehicles to operate in complex industrial environments. They also include a separate, deterministic architecture, independently certified by TÜV SÜD, that defines and enforces the safety boundary.

“Safety is one of the main motivations of the OEMs, as is reducing manual errors or damage caused by manual behavior,” explained Beck. “Vehicle movements need to be precise and to integrate into OEM space constraints. Our system can work alongside factory workers and manually driven vehicles. This enables us to integrate into existing processes and work in all weather conditions.”

A fleet manager gets destinations from the OEM’s back-end systems, defines vehicle routes, and manages communications among automated vehicles, she said.

The value for manufacturers goes beyond individual vehicles, asserted Embotech. Automated movements can support smoother vehicle flow, more stable and flexible operations, and round-the-clock capability independent of shift staffing.

BMW scales from pilot to network deployment

“The 1 million vehicle milestone demonstrates the scale that BMW Group has achieved with Automated Driving In-Plant, spanning different sites, brands, vehicle types, and production and logistics processes,” said Embotech. The partners added that they have demonstrated that the system is precise and reliable enough to scale within BMW‘s live production network.

BMW and Embotech have brought the Automated Driving In-Plant system to about 3,500 vehicle movements a day, with more than 99.5% availability. In manufacturing environments where unexpected downtime can disrupt wider operations, maintaining that level of availability is essential to keeping automated vehicle movements integrated, said Embotech.

Since an initial pilot in 2022, Embotech deployments have expanded to four BMW sites including Dingolfing, Leipzig, and Regensburg in Germany and MINI Plant Oxford in the U.K. The technology supports different use cases in defined production and logistics areas in each factory.

“One million vehicles moved using automated driving technology and the deployment of this technology at four sites to date demonstrates the innovative strength and scaling capabilities of our production network,” said Raymond Wittmann, the member of BMW AG’s board responsible for production. “We recognized the potential of Automated Driving In-Plant early, tested it in a pilot phase, and systematically developed it to series maturity. We are now rolling out this technology worldwide.

“Automated Driving In-Plant is a prime example of how we are translating the vision of the BMW iFACTORY into industrial practice and driving the efficiency, digitalization and intelligent connectivity across our production,” he added.

Embotech said its Munich team has worked closely with BMW to develop supporting tools and processes for deployment, monitoring, diagnosis, and recovery. “Operational experience supports the continuous improvement of Embotech’s perception, prediction, and planning software, helping future deployments and software releases build on what has been learned in live production,” it said.

“What excites us over and above the 1 million milestone is the pace at which that experience is compounding,” said Kyrtatos. “With BMW Group, we completed the first 500,000 automated vehicle movements in 15 months and the next 500,000 in just seven. For Embotech, the next phase is about taking what we have learned into more use cases, sites, customers, and industrial environments.”

“We’re also looking to roll out Automated Driving In-Plant next year at BMW Spartanburg,” Beck said, referring to the South Carolina factory where BMW has tested Figure AI humanoid robots. “We are scaling our solution further across use cases and customers.”

The Xpanner X1 Piling R6 is an automated pile-driving system for utility-scale solar and battery energy storage sites. | Credit: Xpanner

Xpanner today announced the X1 Piling R6, a fully automated pile-driving robot built to autonomously install posts for utility-scale solar and battery energy storage, or BESS, sites. Supervised by a single operator, the system uses high-precision GNSS and onboard sensors to place each pile accurately, helping builders keep pace with new power demand despite a shortage of skilled crews.

The core of the robot is Xpanner’s Everstar R6 crawler base machine. The R6 is equipped with the Santa Fe Springs, Calif.-based company‘s automation stack with onboard sensors and controls to autonomously complete the pile driving process for each post.

Xpanner designs for simplified operation

An operator uploads a plan, then walks X1 Piling R6 machine to the row using a remote control interface. The operator supervises the construction as the machine drives each pile accurately.

The R6 can autonomously navigate to the subsequent pile locations using high-precision GNSS antennas and receivers, precision sensors, and the Xpanner-developed automation controller. One operator can remotely manage the installation process.

“Solar and BESS builders are racing to bring new power online for the grid and for AI data centers, and they can’t find enough skilled crews to keep up,” said Henri Lee, co-founder and CEO of Xpanner. “X1 lets one operator drive every pile plumb with a single touch, keeps people away from the mast, and logs each pile as it goes in. It takes the automation EPCs [engineering, procurement, and construction firms] already trust on PD10 and puts it on a more powerful, more versatile machine.”

X1 connects to Xpanner Connect, the company’s web-based project dashboard. Project teams can load the pile schedule and coordinates, assign machines, and set up a site in minutes.

As X1 works, it records each pile’s position, depth, and plumb and posts it to a live project map, replacing manual counts, phone calls, spreadsheets, and end-of-day reports. Managers can also monitor machine state, cycle counts, and alerts across the fleet without a site visit.

Xpanner said business model is a mixed capex/SaaS subscription model. Customers purchase (or rent) the X1 Piling robot and then license the automation software on a monthly subscription basis for each active technology.

According to the company, the subscription is not tied to a specific project, site, or number of piles driven. Rather, the customer pays for the technology while it is actively being used. Once piling operations or the applicable task is completed, the equipment and technology can be transferred to another project and activated as needed.

Xpanner handles initial installation, calibration, operator training, and technical support, while the contractor provides the equipment operators on-site.

The Xpanner X1 Piling robot autonomously installs the posts for a solar panel farm. | Credit: Xpanner

Key features of the X1 Piling R6 robot

  • Power for hard ground: The system includes a 97 kW (130 hp) engine and a high-frequency hydraulic hammer with up to 1,260 J (929 ft.-lb.) of impact energy and three energy settings to match soil conditions.
  • Fine positioning without tramming: The guide rail slides 11.8 in. (300 mm) forward and back and 19.7 in. (500 mm) left and right, and the upper body rotates 180 degrees, putting the hammer on target from a single setup.
  • Range of pile lengths: The X1 can drive piles up to 23 ft. (7.0 m) long, with a maximum driving depth of 15.7 ft. (4.8 m). Because the hammer lowers near the ground and piles can be driven flush to grade, one machine handles standard tracker piles, short motor piles, and BESS foundation piles without an adapter.
  • Built for the field: Features include a mast that does not need disassembly for transport, a large fuel tank for long shifts, engine auto-idle, a large-capacity cooler, manual override, and e-stop.
  • Multi-function mast (and potential capabilities): DTH drilling, auger drilling, and ground screwing on the same carrier, so one machine can pre-drill and drive.

The X1 Piling R6 is designed to work together with the X1 panel lift, which was released earlier this year, for autonomous solar panel installation.

]]>

Bedrock Robotics automates large excavators to improve construction site economics. | Credit: Bedrock Robotics

San Francisco-based Bedrock Robotics has raised $600 million in Series C funding, co-led by CapitalG and Emergence Capital, at a $4.1 billion valuation. The round brings its total funding to nearly $1 billion as it scales fully autonomous heavy equipment to address nationwide construction labor shortages.

The round included new investors US Innovative Technology Fund (USIT), Bessemer Venture Partners, and Temasek, alongside existing investors 8VC, Georgian, Valor Equity Partners, Xora, Eclipse, Perry Creek Capital, NVIDIA, and others. Bedrock said this will accelerate the deployment of Bedrock-equipped machines across commercial construction sites across the U.S., helping contractors use existing heavy equipment more safely, predictably, and at greater capacity.

The new capital follows a rapid commercial expansion beyond the company’s initial footprint in the West and Central South into the Midwest and South Atlantic. Anchored by a major partnership with Southwest contractor Haydon to automate earthwork in Texas, Bedrock has added regional partners across Minnesota, Florida, Georgia, Missouri, and Virginia—pushing its autonomous retrofits onto live job sites spanning data centers, healthcare facilities, and heavy civil infrastructure.

“We have proven that fully autonomous excavators can perform real work of value alongside the crews and workflows already in place on job sites,” said Boris Sofman, co-founder and CEO of Bedrock Robotics. “The next challenge is delivering that capability to more contractors as a dependable part of how projects get built.”

“This funding allows us to expand deployments, strengthen the field operations behind every machine, and work with more partners as they integrate intelligent systems into everyday work,” he added. “The opportunity is to help the industry’s experienced crews safely take on more projects, deliver with greater consistency, and quickly deliver more of the infrastructure this country needs.”

Sofman told The Robot Report, “New customer demand is very high. We’re responsibly growing into the demand, bringing on new customers we can serve alongside our longtime design partners. We’re scaling across the board, from operations to hardware to supply chain operations, to keep pace with the needs of our customers.”

Bedrock Robotics adds leadership

In the midst of securing new funding, the company also added two new individuals to the management team.

Amy Jones Satrom joins the leadership team as vice president of operations. She brings operations experience from Amazon, Nuro, and Uber to lead the company in the next phase of scaling to meet demand.

“Amy is instrumental in strengthening our operations and building the systems and support that make successful deployments repeatable,” according to Sofman. “She’s still early in her tenure, but her leadership will be central to growing our deployment and production teams and preparing them to support customers across the country.

“Ajay Gummalla, a co-founder and VP of engineering, is also intimately involved on the hardware side of things, adding resilience to our supply chain so we’re ready to build the hardware we need to meet customer demand,” he explained.

Lando Juarez has joined Bedrock Robotics in the role of general counsel. He was formerly head of legal for Uber’s Autonomous Mobility & Delivery business, overseeing commercial partnerships and regulatory pathways.

Submit your innovation now!

Looking to the future of construction

When asked bout how the company is planning to grow, Sofman responded, “Short term, our growth market remains construction. It is a massive market — 4% to 5% of U.S. GDP — so we’re thinking about expanding use cases. Haydon will test our excavators for autonomous trench work.”

“We’re also thinking about automating larger machine models — Haydon and others will explore bulldozers, ADTs, and wheel loaders as possible heavy machines to automate next,” he said. “Long term: We’re looking at the other industries, like mining and agriculture, that are 1) also dealing with labor constraints and 2) use the same kinds of heavy machines GCs do.”

“For 2027, we are relentlessly focused on getting more Bedrock-equipped machines on more job sites around the country,” Sofman continued. “It was just a few months ago that we first launched fully autonomous excavators on live, commercial job sites, just two years after Bedrock came out of stealth. 2027 is about doubling down on that progress, getting to triple-digit machines working autonomously across the country.”

When asked about the installed base and economic opportunity for Bedrock Robotics’ systems, Sofman was more reserved.

“It’s a bit early to give concrete numbers,” said Sofman, “However, given the labor constraints on general contractors, the math pencils out: Imagine a job that can be completed two months faster because autonomous machines are running around the clock, seven days a week.”

“The developer paying 9% interest on a $400 million loan would save $6 million on that project they can invest into future projects,” he observed. “In turn, construction crews and all the downstream trades, like plumbing and electrical, would see an increasing volume of steady work because there are more projects that can be funded.”

Some data on labor constraints that have opened the market for Bedrock:

  • Twenty percent of construction workers are over the age of 55, and estimates suggest that more than 40% of the construction workers will retire in the next five years.

  • Large projects already run an average of 20% over schedule and 80% over budget.

Generative Bionics this week announced plans to build a proprietary, multi-site “Physical AI Data Factory” in Italy. The company said the new 5,000-sq.-m (53,819.5-sq.-ft.) hub will help move humanoid robotics from laboratory demonstrations to reliable industrial deployment.

In addition, Generative Bionics said it hopes to advance European humanoid sovereignty, ensuring that the data, models, and know-how behind Europe’s industrial humanoids are generated, trained and validated on the continent.

“The value that Europe has right now is within its industry, and we have to extract physical AI data in order to train our own models,” Daniele Pucci, the CEO of Generative Bionics, told The Robot Report. “This is a competitive advantage that Europe right now has, because of the automation that we have been putting in place over the last 40 years.”

Generative Bionics said the new facility will be operational by the fourth quarter of 2027. The Genoa, Italy-based company plans to eventually open a second facility elsewhere in Europe and a third serving global markets. Together, the three facilities will reproduce real industrial environments, generate high-fidelity physical data, and connect that data with large-scale simulation.

Building on their strategic technology collaboration, Advanced Micro Devices Inc. will be Generative Bionics’ AI infrastructure partner, and the Physical AI Data Factory network will be powered by AMD Helios. Its rack-scale architecture will provide the compute foundation to process physical and synthetic data, train physical AI models, and run thousands of digital-twin scenario variations in parallel.

Data Factory to test GENE.01 in a range of industries

The Physical AI Data Factory will connect real-world robot operations, simulation and AI development in a continuous real-to-sim-to-real cycle, said Generative Bionics. The company said this will allow it to configure and validate its GENE.01 humanoid robot for specific industrial environments before customer deployment, then feed data from deployed fleets into future training cycles.

Industrial humanoids must learn from the conditions they will encounter at work, noted the Generative Bionics. This requires data that captures contact, force, motion, proximity, temperature, task constraints, and human interaction in realistic operating settings. For GENE.01, the dataset will include vision and motion data as well as signals captured through its full-body multimodal skin.

“A robot is not only vision and is not only language,” said Pucci. “It is position, velocity, acceleration, temperature, and contact forces, so there is a large variety of data that you have to take into account.”

The Data Factory will reproduce environments selected with industrial partners and allow fleets of GENE.01 robots to perform tasks continuously in real-world conditions. These operations will generate high-fidelity physical data for training world action models (WAM) and validating the complete robot system, including perception, control, safety behavior, and task execution, before deployment at customer sites.

Each physical environment and robot configuration will also be recreated as a digital twin. The same tasks can then be repeated across thousands of variations in layout, objects, materials, operating conditions, and failure modes that would be impractical to reproduce physically. Models trained and tested in simulation will be deployed back to the robots for validation, while data from physical operations will feed the next training cycle.

Generative Bionics wants to help find robot ‘ChatGPT moment’

Large language models (LLMs) learn from vast amounts of information available online, noted Generative Bionics. Humanoid robots have no comparable source of data on how to act in the physical world.

The Physical AI Data Factory will create such a source by collecting data as GENE.01 performs industrial tasks and expanding those experiences through digital-twins running on AMD compute.

“We have the ambition of being the European champion in physical AI, and even robotics, designed to scale globally,” said Pucci. “That’s our clear positioning, and for this, we are taking a close look at the supply chain that can supply our future manufacturing.”

“Manufacturing here is divided into three levels: the manufacturing of data, the manufacturing of robots, and the manufacturing of models,” she continued. Pucci said if Europe wants to achieve sovereignty in this area, it needs to invest in all three.

Right now, humanoid robots from China have been garnering a lot of attention with flashy demos and large funding rounds. But, Pucci, notes that this doesn’t mean the country is necessarily ahead of Europe.

“I want to be crystal clear about this. Many of the Chinese robots that are out there are simply not certified to enter industrial settings,” Pucci said. “The narrative that the Chinese solved as the issues is very far from reality.”

“Right now, we believe that many of the existing solutions are basically for entertainment, and this is a market segment that we respect,” she added. “But, Generative Bionics is taking the issue of safety and certification very seriously because we want to go B2B first.”

GENE.01 can be customized for specific applications

Generative Bionics claimed that a few things separate its platform from the average humanoid robot. To start, GENE.01 features full-body tactile sensing.

“It comes naturally to give the humanoid robots the sense of touch, because humanoid robots have to perceive people not only while talking, but also while interacting with them physically,” Pucci said. “That’s why GENE was given this unique multimodal scheme, which can perceive not only the sense of touch but also the sense of proximity.”

Generative Bionics also plans to offer GENE.01 as a base platform that can be customized for different industries.

“We have a clear view that humanoid robots cannot be used for anything that comes to your mind, because a humanoid robot welding in a shipyard cannot be the same as a humanoid robot in healthcare,” noted Pucci. “There is a fundamental difference in the development cycle.”

The company has three levels of customization. “The first one is the AI, because a robot moving boxes does not need the same AI of a robot in healthcare,” said Pucci. “The second is the exterior design. In the shipyard, you have to be resistant against high temperatures, sparks, and powders. The third is the hands and the feet.”

“This is really scalable at the manufacturing level, because you have a common platform, and then you can customize at the end the so-called end of lines at these three levels,” she continued. “This is basically the same approach that you have in automotive.”

Generative Bionics is building on more than 20 years of research, development, and prototyping of humanoids at the Italian Institute of Technology (IIT). The company spun out of IIT in 2024, and IIT has granted it exclusive licenses to key technologies.

Dream Labs said its models learn how the physical world works from video and can control new robots without any data. | Source: Dream Labs

More brains are coming for robots. Dream Labs this week said it has raised $90 million in seed funding. The company also launched Dream API, a publicly available application programming interface to turn a robot’s camera feed and a plain-English instructions into motor commands, even for robots it has never seen before.

Factories worldwide run a record 5 million industrial robots, yet nearly every one is programmed for a single task, and most cannot transfer what they have learned to other machines, noted Dream Labs. Low-cost robots now sell for a few thousand dollars but ship with no built-in intelligence. Teaching one robot one task can take specialists months, and a new task or new hardware often means starting from zero, according to the San Francisco startup.

Dream Labs said its Dream-1 flagship model works across robots from different manufacturers. Trained on video of people performing everyday tasks, it can predict what will happen next and determine the robot’s resulting action. Because it learns from video rather than from a single machine, its capabilities transfer across hardware, Dream Labs claimed.

The company said Dream-1 can control any robot “out of the box” with grippers and zero-shot learning.

“The hardware is ready. What’s been missing is a brain any robot can use,” stated Joel Jang, co-founder and CEO of Dream Labs. “When you get into a rental car, you don’t relearn how to drive. You find the controls, and your past driving experience does the rest.”

“Dream-1 approaches a new robot the same way, so a new robot can do useful work in minutes, not months,” he added. “And instead of edited demos, we’re giving people a working model they can test themselves, mistakes included.”

B Capital and Kindred Ventures led the round. It also included participation from A.Capital, Unusual Ventures, SV Angel, Wing VC, Scribble VC, and Adrian Aoun, among others.

Inside Dream Labs’ product portfolio

Developers and robot enthusiasts can start using Dream Labs’ AI products today. The company said Dream API translates visual inputs and natural language prompts directly into robot actions.

Developers can sign up, connect any robots with grippers, and the robot will carry out the task. Dream Labs runs its models in data centers around the world, so robots respond quickly wherever they are.

The company also offers fine-tuning as a service. For unsupported hardware or new capabilities, developers and robot makers can submit a small batch of demonstration data to receive a tailored model within hours.

Developers also have access to Dream Labs’ robot playground. Anyone with a browser can type commands to a robot in Dream Labs’ San Francisco office and watch it respond live and unedited, no robot purchase required.

“A capable robot arm has gone from the price of a luxury car to the price of a high-end laptop. What it needs now is intelligence,” said Daisy Cai, general partner at B Capital. “This team did some of the defining work in robot learning at NVIDIA. Now anyone with an API key can build on it.”

Startup works with more than 20 hardware partners

Dream Labs supports robots today that cost between about $2,000 and $10,000. Dream-1 needs no extra data to control a two-armed robot with parallel grippers.

For its over 20 hardware partners, Dream Labs said it goes beyond that baseline, refining the model for each robot so it performs at its best. Dream-1 currently handles tabletop tasks such as picking and placing objects and folding laundry, with support for wheeled mobile robots and dexterous hands to follow.

The company said it plans use the new funding primarily for compute as it expands the tasks and robots Dream-1 can handle, and scales to support more users.

“Our customers buy our robots to build things, and the hardest part has always been getting them to do actual work,” said Ryan Chan, co-founder and CEO of MakerMods, which sells $2,000 bimanual robot arms. “With Dream-1, our robot was up and running in a few minutes and attempting tasks we never programmed. We can focus on building better hardware, and our customers get intelligence that keeps improving.”

Arrowfly, an award-winning B2B media and marketing company, today announced that RoboBusiness, the leading robotics industry event for the past 20 years, is being rebranded as Robotics Summit & Expo West, a conference and expo dedicated to the design, deployment, and scaling of commercial robots and businesses. The first event under the new name will be in October 2027 in Santa Clara, Calif.

The timing reflects how the industry has matured. Many robotics companies have moved past the prototype stage, shipping real products into factories, warehouses, and other sites. The questions that define their work are no longer only technical. They are about design for manufacturing, bringing products to market, implementation, managing growing fleets, and providing service and support. Robotics Summit & Expo West will help industry professionals meet increasing demand for intelligent systems across sectors.

“The robotics industry has matured, and the hardest problems have grown with it,” said Steve Crowe, executive editor of The Robot Report and chair of the Robotics Summit. “For 20 years, RoboBusiness brought this community together. Robotics Summit & Expo West will serve that community by sharing lessons from industry leaders on how to move from a pilot that works to a product deployed across multiple sites and building a business that can support it.”

Robotics Summit & Expo West is organized around the questions that define the post-prototype stage of a robotics company:

Deployment at scale: What changes when a robot moves from a controlled pilot to multiple live sites, including integration, fleet management, remote monitoring, and autonomous operations in increasingly unstructured environments.

Go-to-market and commercial strategy: How robotics companies are responding to market demand and structuring pricing, sales, and channel strategies for products that combine hardware, software, and services.

Field data and product decisions: How real-world performance data flows back into product iteration and AI model evolution. Ongoing service and support, whether directly or through partners, is also key to demonstrating a return on investment.

Investment and growth: How investors evaluate robotics companies, and how founding teams can build businesses that last.

The conference program includes keynotes with industry and thought leaders, sessions focused on the latest technical and business topics, insightful panel discussions, and a curated expo floor. Attendees can learn from the founders, operators, and investors who are shaping the future of robotics.

One mission. Two conversations

The rebrand clarifies Arrowfly’s robotics event portfolio. Robotics Summit & Expo Boston (June 2–3, 2027, John B. Hynes Convention Center), the flagship East Coast show, focuses on the core technical and engineering challenges of building robotic systems. Robotics Summit & Expo West focuses on scaling the product and the company behind it. Together, the two events serve the full lifecycle of designing, building, and bringing a robotics product to market.

“Deployment does not end the development process. It changes who is asking the questions,” said Amanda Buehner, senior vice president of sales & strategy, engineering, at Arrowfly. “The engineer designing a new mobile robot and the operations leader managing robots across a warehouse network are both essential to this industry. They need different conversations. That is what the Robotics Summit lineup now provides.”

Robotics hardware, software, and solution providers looking to reach the engineers, product leaders, and executives scaling robotics can learn about sponsorship and exhibit opportunities by contacting Arrowfly’s robotics team.

The post London’s Querio launches with €4.48 million to help companies tackle conflicting answers across AI tools appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Querio, a London-based analytics platform for data teams and their AI agents, has launched today with €4.48 million ($5 million) in total funding. 

Its investors include BMW i Ventures, which led the company’s Seed financing, alongside LAUNCH, the fund run by Jason Calacanis, Haatch Ventures, Araya, Forum Ventures, and Secways.

“Companies want to use AI with their data, but they need to trust the answer. Querio lets data teams hand more of the work to AI agents while a person stays in charge of every change that reaches the business,” said Javier Bonilla, co-founder and CTO at Querio. 

Founded in 2024 by Rami Abi Habib (CEO) and Bonilla (CTO), Querio is an AI analytics platform that helps data teams give the whole company consistent answers in the AI tools it already uses. It keeps a company’s reports, definitions, and analysis in the data team’s GitHub and claims to give business users consistent answers in Claude, ChatGPT, and Slack, with the data team reviewing every change. 

According to the company, it was launched to address the growing challenge of keeping answers consistent across tools as employees turn to AI assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT for business questions. 

It says that when each tool uses a different version of the company’s numbers, people get conflicting answers, and data teams spend their time reconciling them instead of doing new work.

Querio claims to give data teams one place to define what the company’s numbers mean, and keeps that work in the team’s own GitHub rather than locked inside a vendor’s product. 

“For thirty years, analytics tools have kept a company’s logic inside the vendor’s product, where it’s hard to move and hard for AI to work with. Now everyone is asking data questions in Claude, Slack and wherever else they work, and they get three different revenue numbers. We built Querio so the data team owns that logic, and every AI tool in the company answers from it,” said Abi Habib, co-founder and CEO of Querio. 

The UK startup highlighted that business users can ask questions in Claude, ChatGPT or Slack and get the same answer each time. It further notes that when the business changes, Querio’s AI agent updates the affected reports and definitions, and the data team approves each change before anyone sees it.

“Say sales renames a field in the CRM. The revenue dashboard breaks, the Slack bot says no deals closed last week and Claude gives a third number. With Querio, the agent spots the change, fixes everything that depends on it and sends the data team one update to approve. After that, every tool gives the same answer,” Abi Habib added.

Querio is SOC 2 Type II certified and HIPAA- and GDPR-compliant. It also said it does not train on customer data and maintains no-training and no-storage agreements with its AI model providers. It works with companies including OpenVPN and agree.com.

]]> Impress, a Spanish digital orthodontics network, has signed a €40 million venture debt loan with the European Investment Bank (EIB) to scale up investments in its AI platform across its network of more than 110 clinics worldwide. The loan will also accelerate the company’s expansion plans across Europe.

This latest agreement also follows Impress’s over €110 million financing announcement in 2024, which supported its European expansion following the acquisition of DrSmile.

“For years, patients have had to choose between expensive orthodontics with constant clinic visits, or at-home solutions without adequate medical follow-up. At Impress, we were born to close that gap. Our technology features an artificial intelligence engine powered by a global database of 500,000 patients, which allows us to multiply the efficiency of our clinics ten times, reduce in-person visits by 80%, and make quality medical care more accessible.

“The backing of the EIB represents a seal of guarantee in the HealthTech companies’ ecosystem in Europe, confirms our vision, and places us in an advantageous position to consolidate our model in the region,” says Vladimir Lupenko, co-founder and CEO of Impress.

Impress’s financing comes amid a series of European investments in digital dentistry and AI-enabled healthcare in 2026.

In France, Paris-based DentalMonitoring secured €84 million to expand its AI-powered orthodontic monitoring platform, while Montpellier-based Lupin Dental raised €15 million for dental robotics. Belgium’s Relu also attracted €1.51 million for AI-powered dental workflows.

In Spain, Madrid-based Tucuvi raised €17 million for its voice-AI healthcare platform, while Barcelona’s Health Force secured €4.2 million for hospital automation.

Together with Impress’s €40 million venture debt loan, these announcements represent approximately €161.7 million in reported financing, spanning equity investments and debt.

“The digital transformation of the healthcare sector offers significant opportunities to improve the quality and efficiency of services provided to citizens. This operation reflects the EIB’s commitment to supporting innovative European growth companies like Impress that leverage AI to build cutting-edge solutions and expand their footprint across Europe, reinforcing EU leadership in HealthTech innovation,” adds María Romano, Head of the EIB Group Office in Spain.

Founded in Barcelona in 2019 by Vladimir Lupenko, Diliara Lupenko and Khaled Kasem, Impress is an invisible orthodontics and medical technology company. They offer a model that combines in-person care in specialised clinics with continuous monitoring through its AI-powered technology platform.

The company currently operates in 10 countries across Europe and the United States, with more than 110 clinics and 500,000 patients treated globally. In Spain, it has 22 clinics.

On the technology front, today’s investment will drive the development of Impress’s proprietary platform, a comprehensive AI-based healthcare ecosystem designed to unify patient treatment from start to finish.

]]> Europe’s startups have been riding a wave of innovation, creating numerous applications of generative and agentic AI. This innovation has explored the art of the possible, but it has also flooded the world with slop. Content is awash with it, whether it is LinkedIn posts or quotidian corporate drivel.

The slop extends to legal work

AI was supposed to make work easier, but now many are grappling with what Jamie Bartlett, author and BBC journalist, describes as “the burden of AI clog“. Cleaning up this mess means that AI is not saving time, but is actually creating more work.

The slop extends to the legal domain, with contract negotiations and other legal work now being absorbed by a lengthy review process because of AI. Even the bodies that are supposed to be drafting the laws are swimming in slop. In the US, for example, the Office of the Legislative Counsel, is reportedly overwhelmed by the error-riddled drafts that AI has generated.

The problem isn’t AI per se

Advances in LegalTech in Europe, and beyond, means there are many tools to assist with legal work. Despite this, however, their output is of varying quality. And some law firms still don’t have a proper policy in place for how employees use AI, which means some teams are relying on general LLMs (like ChatGPT or Claude) for their drafting and reviewing.

As contracts are amended in negotiations, much of the document is struck through and sent back saturated with red lines. AI editors are ripping and replacing much of the content, and the changes usually lack insight and relevance.

This is hardly the way to engage in a negotiation, and the trigger-happy nature of the tools is likely to aggravate the other party. Judgement and discretion have been lost in the process. Many tools don’t know the difference between dogmatically applying the letter of the law and letting things go for the sake of progressing a negotiation.

Unnecessary redlining can be stopped

This, however, is a problem that Europe’s startups can solve. There are ways to ensure that legal work doesn’t descend into slop, and to prevent the revisions turning into an infinite ping pong match between AI agents.

The focus instead needs to be on judicious editing, where the tool knows when to leave something alone. The amendments should be minimal, and these should be aligned to a well-defined playbook.

This playbook sets out a firm’s position, policies and approach and sets parameters for what is, and isn’t, acceptable. The tool scans for compliance issues, conflicts and highlights areas of difference. It can then make suggested edits that align with this well-defined playbook and offer a best-case scenario for the company, or firm.

This approach is more likely to bridge the gap between the parties and get to a consensus quicker, without the need for human intervention.

AI should be a blessing, not a burden

When used correctly, legal AI can be a blessing for companies and means more work can be done in-house before calling in outside counsel. Such tools can be used as mediation portals, where differences of position are highlighted and evaluated first instead of text being ruthlessly red-lined.

The excessive redlining needs to stop, as does the AI slop and the AI clog burden it creates. At the moment, users are putting up with it albeit complaining about the extra work that AI creates. Soon, however, the slop won’t be tolerated.

We expect the bar to be raised of what AI-enabled work should look like. Expectations will shift and users will soon demand AI tools that edit in a way that is precise, relevant and insightful.

]]> Naboo, a Paris-based EventTech scale-up, has joined forces with UK specialist pro-ven, bringing together two of the Meetings and Events (M&E) sector’s prominent names. 

Starting today, pro-ven becomes Naboo UK. Together, the combined entity now oversees €269 million ($300 million) in meetings and events worldwide. The acquisition was financed through an equal split of equity and debt. The move follows Naboo’s €58.7 million Series B funding round earlier this year, led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and existing investors Notion Capital, ISAI, and Ternel.

“The future category leader in the M&E spend management market will be a pure player. Both event planners and procurement leaders have very high expectations in terms of user experience, embedded compliance, payment simplification, spend analytics and transparency. It cannot be achieved as a side business by TMCs who are still very much focused on transforming the transient travel experience. Together with pro-ven, that is the leader we are building,” said Maxime Eduardo, co-founder and CEO of Naboo.

Founded in 2022 by Eduardo, Antoine Servant, Lucien Bredin, and Jean-Louis Villeminot, Naboo is a platform for booking, managing, and running corporate events, also known as MICE (Meetings, Incentives, Conferences, and Exhibitions). Its offering spans venue sourcing, AI-assisted procurement, corporate payment cards, accounts payable, and event planning tools for organisers and participants.

The company aims to replace the fragmented event tools with its AI operating system, which uses intelligent agents to handle sourcing, quote comparisons, contract review, and payment processing automatically. According to Naboo, its platform delivers an average saving of 12% per event for clients, which includes Google, Meta, Microsoft, Siemens, as well as a quarter of the French CAC 40 index under exclusive contracts.

Established in 2005, pro-ven has spent two decades building deep relationships with enterprise clients across the UK, Europe, and globally. Its expertise spans venue and supplier sourcing, rate negotiation, approval workflows, centralised invoicing, and lodge card management. The tie-up pairs Naboo’s technological scale with proven client expertise in the UK market, where the former has been expanding since opening a London office in 2025 and has signed clients such as KPMG and HSBC.

“I am incredibly excited for our clients and our team to make such a step into the AI-native world, which I believe is the right technology to create a world leader in the M&E market,” said Julian Laxon, founder and Managing Director of pro-ven, who will continue in his role to help as Naboo builds out its UK presence.

pro-ven has 20 employees, and Naboo said it plans to retain everyone to support its exponential growth in the UK market. 

“With Naboo, we are now able to address our clients’ needs for global coverage with equal quality, anywhere in the world. This is the direction our clients’ booking communities and procurement leads are clearly taking: one single vendor of record, anywhere in the world, to cover all the complex elements of venue find, event management and payment,” he added.

The corporate meetings and events sector is estimated at €358 billion ($400 billion) globally, and according to Naboo, the sector is the last major category of enterprise spend that has not yet been digitised. It says the sector has been marked by tension between event organisers looking for experience and agility and procurement and finance teams seeking visibility, compliance, and cost control.

With AI, Naboo says it is economically viable to bridge that gap for every size of event, including the smaller bookings that escaped procurement oversight. The market is reacting to this change with AMEX GBT acquired by Long Lake while Navan acquired Reed & Mackay and partnered with BoomPop.

“We are a service company. Service-as-a-software: it means our software absorbs the operational complexity – the admin, the workflows, the manual steps – so our talents can spend their time on what actually matters: the relationship,” added Eduardo.

The acquisition of pro-van comes weeks after Naboo unveiled a new brand identity in October and opened its first Asia-Pacific office in Singapore. The company has raised €90 million ($100 million) in the past three years) and now aims to exceed €900 million ($1 billion) in business volume by 2027.

Elsewhere in Europe, 2026 funding for software serving wealth managers and financial advisers has included Copenhagen-based Performativ’s €11.96 million Series A, TODAY’s €2.8 million Seed round, and Zurich-based Aisot Technologies’ €2.13 million Seed extension.

AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ Aerospace Global News Tue, 27 Oct 2026 16:32:38 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/cropped-AGN_Icon_Jet-32x32.png AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ 32 32 First Canadian F-35As arrive as Ottawa considers Gripen fighter purchase https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/canada-first-f35a-arrive/ Tue, 27 Oct 2026 17:07:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54454 The first two Canadian CF-35s have been officially handed over for training in Arizona ahead of the first F-35s expected to arrive in Canada in 2028.

The post First Canadian F-35As arrive as Ottawa considers Gripen fighter purchase appeared first on AGN.

]]> The first two Canadian F-35As (Canadian designation CF-35As) have been received at Luke Air Force Base, where Canadian pilots can start training ahead of F-35s arriving in Canada.

Over the weekend, the Royal Canadian Air Force posted, “The RCAF received its first two CF-35As yesterday at Luke Air Force Base in Arizona. The future of air and space power is built on more than equipment alone.”

The announcement follows the first CF-35A (production number AR-1) completing its maiden flight at Lockheed Martin’s Fort Worth, Texas facility in September 2026.

The initial eight aircraft are expected to arrive at Luke Air Force Base during 2026 and 2027. The first aircraft are scheduled to arrive in Canada (4 Wing Cold Lake, Alberta) in late 2028.

The RCAF received its first two CF35As yesterday at Luke Air Force Base in Arizona. The future of air and space power is built on more than equipment alone. https://t.co/mieJL6YDtQ

— Royal Canadian Air Force (@RCAF_ARC) October 23, 2026

Main deliveries are to take place between 2028 and 2032, with Canada targeting Initial Operational Capability (IOC) in 2029 and Full Operational Capability (FOC) around 2033.

Canada’s F-35 continues despite the ongoing review

Despite the ongoing geopolitical drama between the United States and Canada, and Canada’s potential looming Saab Gripen fighter jet purchase, its programme to acquire F-35As (CF-35s) remains on track.

For now, Canada retains its programme of record for 88 F-35As, which are badly needed to replace its fast-aging fleet of CF-18 legacy Hornets. Debate is currently ongoing in Canada about acquiring a mixed fleet of F-35s and Gripens.

Conversation in Ottawa is not about canceling the order for F-35s, but there is debate about reducing it. Canada has committed to the first 16 aircraft, and CBC News reports it is quietly making the advance payments on the next batch of 14 aircraft.

This indicates that Canada has taken steps to preserve production positions for at least another 14 aircraft, although the government has not confirmed a commitment to procure them. If true, it would suggest Canada has committed to at least 30 F-35s.

One of Canada’s key challenges is meeting its NORAD commitments. Requirements relating to interoperability, security and intelligence sharing played a significant role in the fighter competition and contributed to the withdrawal of some competing aircraft.

NORAD requirements were a reason why Airbus (Eurofighter) and Dassault (Rafale) previously withdrew from Canada’s fighter jet competition.

At the time, in 2018, Defense News stated that Dassault’s withdrawal was “over concerns that interoperability and intelligence sharing requirements were too extensive.”

Saab may build Gripen fighter jets in Canada to speed Ukraine deliveries Saab may build Gripen fighter jets in Canada to speed Ukraine deliveries

Moving towards a mixed F-35 and Gripen fighter jet fleet

In June 2026, CBC News wrote, “According to various sources, the federal government would still be looking at a fleet of 72 to 88 F-35s, even if it moves forward with the Gripen.”

It added that Ottawa is exploring a purchase of 72 Gripen E, with negotiations ongoing with Saab about substantial workshare in Canada for these aircraft.

Commentators have linked the GlobalEye decision to the emerging Gripen discussion, particularly because Saab’s proposed Canadian industrial model could potentially extend beyond the AEW&C programme.

Canada could eventually acquire a fleet of 140 fighter jets. Supporters of a mixed fleet argue it could allow Canada to maintain a fighter force optimised for NORAD missions while also diversifying its suppliers and industrial partnerships.

A leaked report suggested that the F-35 outperformed the Gripen during Canadian competitions ‘by a mile ‘, achieving a ‘near perfect’ score of 95% vs 33% for the Gripen E.

Canada is having to balance a range of industrial, political, geopolitical, and military concerns with its fighter jet programme.

]]> Boeing pushes 737 production target into 2027 despite record $745bn backlog https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/boeing-pushes-737-production-target-2027/ Tue, 27 Oct 2026 16:16:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54670 Boeing's 737 production ramp-up has slipped into 2027 despite certification progress and a record $745 billion backlog, highlighting ongoing supply-chain challenges.

The post Boeing pushes 737 production target into 2027 despite record $745bn backlog appeared first on AGN.

]]> Boeing will not achieve its planned 737 production rate of 47 aircraft per month until early 2027, chief executive Kelly Ortberg has said, as the manufacturer continues to face supply-chain constraints despite record demand.

Speaking to CNBC following the release of Boeing’s third-quarter results, Ortberg said the company had hoped to achieve the milestone during 2026. It now expects it to take “into early next year”.

The delay comes despite continued progress across Boeing’s commercial aircraft programmes and a record order backlog.

Record backlog and certification milestones

In its third-quarter results published today (27 October), Boeing reported revenue of $24.2 billion, operating cash flow of $1.5 billion and a company-wide backlog of $745 billion – the highest in its history.

The manufacturer also completed two major certification milestones for the 737 MAX family. The 737-7 received amended type certification from the Federal Aviation Administration during the third quarter, while the 737-10 was certified in October.

“Recent milestones, including certification of the 737-7 and 737-10 and selection to design and build the Navy’s sixth-generation fighter aircraft, are important steps as we continue building on our progress,” said Ortberg.

Commercial aircraft business remains under pressure

Boeing’s Commercial Airplanes division generated $10.7 billion in revenue during the quarter, down 3% year-on-year, and posted an operating loss of $697 million.

The company said results were affected by a less favourable mix of aircraft deliveries, rising costs linked to increasing production rates and ongoing supply-chain pressures.

Boeing nevertheless continued to make progress across its commercial programmes. The company said the 737 programme continues to progress towards a stabilised production rate of 47 aircraft per month.

The 787 Dreamliner remains at a production rate of eight aircraft per month. The company also said the 777X remains on track for first delivery in 2027.

Despite the challenges, Boeing delivered 161 aircraft during the quarter and 475 aircraft during the first nine months of the year. The company also booked 300 net orders, including deals with Turkish Airlines, Ethiopian Airlines and Lufthansa.

The commercial aircraft backlog now stands at more than 6,300 aircraft worth a record $612 billion.

Defence and services support recovery

Revenue at Boeing Defense, Space & Security rose 15% to $7.9 billion, with operating earnings increasing to $492 million. During the quarter, Boeing was selected by the US Navy to design, build and deliver the next-generation F/A-XX fighter aircraft, although the award has not yet been added to backlog figures.

Financial performance improves

Boeing reported a net loss of $116 million for the quarter, a significant improvement from the $5.3 billion loss recorded in the same period a year earlier.

The company generated free cash flow of $464 million and ended the quarter with $20.7 billion in cash and marketable securities.

In a message to employees released alongside the results, Ortberg acknowledged progress but said more work remained.

“Expectations are rising, and they should. We have a stronger foundation than a year ago, but we also have more work to do to deliver on our backlog, strengthen our culture, and improve how we work every day.”

]]> British Airways crew reports near miss with UFO during New York flight https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/british-airways-ufo-encounter-heathrow/ Tue, 27 Oct 2026 15:47:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54637 A British Airways Boeing 777 bound for New York came within an estimated 50ft of an unidentified flying object (UFO) shortly after departing Heathrow, with investigators later classifying the incident as a serious risk of collision.

The post British Airways crew reports near miss with UFO during New York flight appeared first on AGN.

]]> A mystery object spotted by the crew of a British Airways flight to New York has been classified as a serious air safety incident after passing within an estimated 50ft of the aircraft shortly after take-off from Heathrow.

The aircraft was climbing through 5,800 feet near Guildford, Surrey, when the crew spotted what appeared to be a silver, metallic object travelling in the opposite direction. They described it as reflective and about the “size of four toasters”. The pilots thought it might be a drone. 

The UK Airprox Board investigated the report in September and gave it a Category A rating, meaning there had been a serious risk of collision. The case record describes the object as being “too close for comfort.”

British Airways addresses the UFO sighting

The crew reported the sighting to air traffic control at around 12:08 UTC. The incident did not require evasive action, and the flight continued to New York, where it landed on schedule.

A British Airways spokesperson told The Independent: “We take matters such as these extremely seriously, and our pilots report these incidents so authorities can investigate them and take appropriate action.”

The Airprox Board considered the report at its September meeting, recording it as case 2026127. Investigators could not find matching radar contact for the object, and were unable to identify it.

More unidentified objects reported near UK airports

The Airprox Board’s September 2026 records contain other reports of unidentified flying objects spotted near passenger aircraft.

On 21 June, an Airbus A320 crew departing Heathrow saw a large object they believed could be a drone, although investigators could not confirm.

There were also sightings reported by Boeing 787 crews flying near Rochdale and Birmingham.

A UFO is simply an object in the sky that has not been identified. It does not imply that the flying object is of extraterrestrial origin. Some past sightings have been explained as aircraft, balloons, satellites or natural phenomena. 

The UK National Archives holds records of UFO sightings reported to the Ministry of Defence, including many accounts from airline pilots.

British Airways pilots have reported UFO sightings before

In January 1995, pilots aboard a BA Boeing 737 flying from Milan to Manchester reported seeing a wedge-shaped object with lights pass near their aircraft.

The 737 was descending through 4,000 feet when the object appeared on its right-hand side. The first officer reportedly ducked as it went past.

The Civil Aviation Authority’s Joint Airmiss Working Group investigated the sighting but could not explain it. Ministry of Defence records released later showed that military aircraft had been ruled out. The MOD found no evidence of a threat to UK air defences.

Another BA crew reported an unusual sighting over Ireland on 9 November 2018. The pilots were flying a Boeing 787 from Montreal to Heathrow on flight BA94 when they spotted a bright object moving rapidly near their aircraft.

They contacted Shannon air traffic control to ask whether there were military exercises in the area. Other pilots, including a Virgin Atlantic crew, also reported seeing unusual lights.

The Irish Aviation Authority investigated without reaching a definitive conclusion, though meteors entering the atmosphere were one possible explanation.

For the British Airways crew departing Heathrow, as with similar previous UFO sightings, the object the pilots saw remains a mystery.

]]> Aeroméxico targets further European growth from regional airports amid strong demand https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/aeromexico-europe-flights-growth-airports-routes-world/ Tue, 27 Oct 2026 14:58:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54635 The carrier’s latest plans include a new Guadalajara–Paris service in April 2027, following the launch of Monterrey–Paris and the addition of Mexico City–Milan next March.

The post Aeroméxico targets further European growth from regional airports amid strong demand appeared first on AGN.

]]> Aeroméxico is seeking to launch flights to additional European destinations as it broadens its international network beyond Mexico City, with Guadalajara and Monterrey among the airports it sees as potential secondary hubs. 

The carrier’s latest plans include a new Guadalajara–Paris service in April 2027, following the launch of Monterrey–Paris and the addition of Mexico City–Milan next March.

European routes ‘so successful’ Aeroméxico is looking for more

“Our European routes have been so successful that we’re looking for new destinations in Europe,” Manuel Moreno Lagos, Aeroméxico’s director of network planning, said at Routes World 2026 in Frankfurt.

Aeroméxico’s expansion ambitions come as the Mexican flag carrier seeks to build on demand from cities outside the capital – one of the largest cities in the world – rather than relying solely on its main hub. 

“We’re looking to expand,” Moreno Lagos said. “We’re not just in Mexico City. We’re also looking for opportunities from Monterrey, and from Guadalajara.”

Guadalajara and Monterrey support network expansion

The airline plans to operate Guadalajara–Paris three times weekly during the summer 2027 season. 

Moreno Lagos said the decision followed the impressive performance of the Monterrey–Paris flight, which Aeroméxico launched as a seasonal service and announced in July would be extended into the winter schedule. 

Aeroméxico is also adding Mexico City–Milan in 2027, giving it a second Italian destination in addition to Rome. 

The carrier has launched Barcelona from Mexico City and described its European routes as performing strongly.

Aeroméxico serves major capitals including Madrid, Amsterdam, London and Paris, however there are gaps in its network map, including Germany, Portugal, and eastern and northern Europe.  

Moreno Lagos told delegates at the Routes World event that his airline was interested in both new links and additional frequencies on existing routes, and was seeking proposals from airports and their partners.

Read more: Flights to Mexico disrupted after cartel violence sparks airport closures Read more: Flights to Mexico disrupted after cartel violence sparks airport closures

Hub economics shape Aeroméxico’s route choices

Mexico City remains central to the airline’s strategy. Aeroméxico operates 45 domestic destinations from the capital, connecting them with its international network. 

But the airport’s elevation – 2,230 metres (7,316 feet) above sea level – creates operational challenges, including longer take-off requirements and limitations on aircraft range and payload.

Those performance limitations affect route planning, particularly for long-haul services. Aeroméxico operates Boeing 787s on its longer intercontinental routes, including services to South America and Asia.

However, its flights to Tokyo and Seoul make a stop in Monterrey to refuel, and passengers can remain on board while additional travellers can join. 

Aeroméxico seeks airport data and commercial support

For prospective routes, Moreno Lagos said the airline was serious about exploring growth opportunities, and had requested detailed information from airport partners, including data on unserved and underserved markets, potential demand and opportunities to increase frequency. 

The carrier operates more than 550 flights a day across 137 routes, serving 25 countries in the Americas, Europe and Asia. 

The United States is a key market for Aeroméxico, and its partnership with Delta has helped the carrier broaden its reach there.

“We have had a joint cooperation agreement since 2017 with them,” Moreno Lagos said, adding that “that cooperation agreement has allowed us to have a stronger presence in the US.”

Aeroméxico and Delta jointly operate more than 1,600 weekly flights to over 60 destinations.

]]> Electra’s hybrid-electric EL2 aircraft lands at Manhattan Heliport in a regional aviation milestone https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/electra-el2-operations-manhattan-heliport/ Tue, 27 Oct 2026 14:01:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54613 The company said that the operation marked the first time a conventional fixed-wing aircraft without vertical take-off capability had landed at the heliport.

The post Electra’s hybrid-electric EL2 aircraft lands at Manhattan Heliport in a regional aviation milestone appeared first on AGN.

]]> Electra Aero has taken another step toward its vision for airport-independent regional aviation after its EL2 hybrid-electric demonstrator landed and took off from a Lower Manhattan heliport.

The demonstration took place on 26 October at Downtown Skyport, a waterfront facility operated by Skyports Infrastructure.

Electra believes the event marked the first time a conventional fixed-wing aircraft without vertical take-off capability had landed at the heliport.

The flight formed part of the company’s Life Beyond Runways programme, which aims to demonstrate how aircraft capable of operating within extremely short distances could open new regional routes without requiring conventional airport runways.

The technology is intended to underpin Electra’s larger EL9, a nine-passenger aircraft the company hopes to introduce into commercial service around 2030.

Blown-lift technology enables ultra-short operations

Electra’s EL2 Goldfinch is a two-seat technology demonstrator designed to test the company’s approach to ultra-short take-off and landing (USTOL).

Its defining feature is blown-lift technology, which directs airflow from electrically driven propellers over the wings and large flaps.

This increases lift at low airspeeds, allowing the aircraft to become airborne after a much shorter ground roll than a conventional aeroplane would require.

Once airborne and established in cruise, the aircraft can retract its flaps and transition to normal fixed-wing flight.

We said where we land next might surprise you. The third era of aviation just landed in Lower Manhattan. ✈️ Electra’s hybrid-electric, fixed-wing Ultra Short aircraft just completed a historic flight demonstration at the Downtown Skyport. No runway required. This latest chapter in Life Beyond Runways shows what becomes possible when an airplane needs just 150 feet to take off and land. Regional flights that reach city centers. Journeys that save hours. Military operations that can reach places conventional aircraft cannot. This is the promise of Direct Aviation – bringing flight closer to the places people need to go. Read more: https://t.co/Il1lRX76z3 #LifeBeyondRunways #Electra #DirectAviation #UltraShort #EL9

— Electra.aero (@ElectraAero) October 26, 2026

Electra’s target for the production-oriented EL9 is a take-off and landing ground roll of approximately 150 feet (46 metres). That could enable operations from suitably prepared heliports and other confined locations that would be unsuitable for most conventional aircraft.

The Manhattan demonstration follows previous appearances by the EL2 at locations including Charleston, South Carolina, Atlantic City, New Jersey, and Snowshoe Mountain Resort in West Virginia.

Electra has also demonstrated operations using helicopter-style instrument procedures at Roanoke-Blacksburg Regional Airport in Virginia, exploring how ultra-short aircraft could integrate with existing aviation infrastructure.

Also read: Electra proves its Ultra Short aircraft can operate from heliports and taxiways Also read: Electra proves its Ultra Short aircraft can operate from heliports and taxiways

A different approach to regional travel

Electra calls its proposed operating model ‘Direct Aviation’. Rather than concentrating regional services around major airports, the concept envisages flights connecting passengers through a distributed network of smaller departure and arrival points.

Potential locations include heliports, small airfields, waterfront facilities, fields and other suitable sites. The objective is to reduce the time passengers spend travelling to airports and navigating busy terminals.

According to Electra’s own market analysis, its proposed approach could save travellers approximately three hours and 45 minutes on journeys between New York and Boston, three hours and 30 minutes between New York and Washington, D.C., and 45 minutes between New York and Philadelphia.

These figures are company estimates, rather than demonstrated savings from an operating passenger service.

For Downtown Skyport, the demonstration illustrates how existing helicopter facilities might eventually accommodate additional forms of regional transport.

Robbie Ladov, Skyports Infrastructure’s general manager for US heliports and vertiports, said the aircraft could expand the facility’s potential connections beyond conventional helicopter journeys.

Electra chief executive Marc Allen similarly emphasised the possibility of using existing infrastructure instead of constructing new runways.

EL9 development and certification

The EL2 is a technology demonstrator, while the larger EL9 is intended to become Electra’s commercial product.

The planned EL9 will accommodate up to nine passengers and use eight electric motors powered by a hybrid-electric system incorporating batteries and a turbine-driven generator.

The generator is designed to supply electricity during flight and support battery recharging.

Electra has published a projected cruise speed of 175 knots and a maximum ferry range of 1,100 nautical miles with reserves.

Its certification announcement also describes the aircraft as being designed for routes of up to 330 nautical miles, illustrating the distinction between maximum ferry capability and intended passenger operations.

In July 2026, Electra announced that the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) had established the EL9’s certification basis, an important early step in the aircraft’s type-certification programme.

The company is targeting a first flight in late 2027 or early 2028, with commercial entry into service planned for 2030.

Electra reports more than 2,200 letters of intent from over 60 commercial customers, including airlines and helicopter operators. It also has relationships with US government customers, including the Air Force, Army, Navy and NASA.

Demonstration success is only the beginning

Despite the progress, the Manhattan flight does not by itself establish that regular passenger operations from heliports are commercially or operationally ready. The EL9 must still progress through development, testing and certification.

Operators will also need suitable infrastructure, regulatory approvals and viable routes before the concept can become a routine transport option.

Nevertheless, the demonstration highlights an alternative approach to regional aviation: using fixed-wing efficiency while reducing dependence on conventional runways.

If Electra can translate its demonstrator’s performance into a certified passenger aircraft, existing urban heliports and other compact sites could become useful links in a broader regional transport network.

]]> Helsing unveils new interceptors to counter Russia’s jet-powered attack drones https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/helsing-contra-ai-air-defence/ Tue, 27 Oct 2026 13:05:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54580 Helsing has unveiled an AI-powered air-defence system and two new interceptors designed to counter mass drone and missile attacks, including the growing threat posed by fast jet-powered drones.

The post Helsing unveils new interceptors to counter Russia’s jet-powered attack drones appeared first on AGN.

]]> Germany defence-tech company Helsing has unveiled Contra, an AI-powered autonomous air-defence system designed to counter large-scale drone and missile attacks. It has also introduced two new interceptor missiles built to tackle the fast-emerging threat of jet-powered drones.

The announcement comes as European defence planners grapple with Russia’s increasing use of high-speed one-way attack drones and cruise missiles, which are proving more challenging to detect and defeat.

Contra: The AI-enabled brain

In discussions about drone interceptors, the importance of identifying, tracking, and targeting the threats is often overlooked. The faster drones get, and the more there are, the more time is compressed and the more information there is to process.

Contra is being designed to help address this problem. Helsing described Contra as an AI-controlled autonomous air defence system designed to protect countries from scaled drone and missile attacks. The system is built to draw “high capability from affordable, mass-producible hardware.”

Contra is designed to defeat Geran-type threats. The company claims the autonomous AI system enables the detection and engagement of hundreds or thousands of drone and missile threats at the same time. It is able to fuse the information into a single picture.

Today we are unveiling Contra, an AI-controlled autonomous air defence system designed to protect countries from scaled drone and missile attacks. Alongside Contra, two new interceptors: AD-1 Inferno to counter jet-powered threats. AD-2 Ambush to counter high-altitude threats. https://t.co/Z9HE2UB2ft

— Helsing (@HelsingAI) October 26, 2026

Helsing named its Altra C2 platform as the foundation of the system. Altra is an AI-powered, software-defined command-and-control (C2) and recce-strike platform, with users retaining “full control over decision-making and prioritisation.”

The new Helsing interceptor missiles

Helsing also announced two new interceptor weapons with advanced radar seekers: AD-1 Inferno and AD-2 Ambush. These are intended to “outmatch” and “outrun” the fastest jet-powered drone and cruise missile threats.

The AD-1 Inferno is a jet-powered interceptor capable of aerial loitering, swarming, and repeated re-engagements.

Meanwhile, AD-2 Ambush is a much higher-end solution. It is a solid-rocket-motor (SRM) missile for rapid intercepts, reaching Mach 2.5 and a range of 20km+.

Its Mach 2.5 top speed is substantially higher than the reported speeds of Russia’s jet-powered Geran drones. The Geran-4’s speed is reported as roughly 320–500 km/h, and the Geran-5 is around 450–600 km/h depending on variant and estimate.

These interceptors are designed to receive mid-course guidance from the Contra radar ground stations. Contra is being built to integrate third-party interceptors, cUAV lasers, and other counter-drone systems “in a matter of days.”

Russia builds vast jet-drone launch base in six weeks as attacks on Ukraine surge Russia builds vast jet-drone launch base in six weeks as attacks on Ukraine surge

The need to counter faster Russian jet-powered drones

In its announcement, Helsing explicitly referred to Russia’s transition to much faster jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 Sahed-style drones as use cases for its new interceptors. It notes these pose a security risk not only for Ukraine but also for Europe.

Ukraine’s domestically produced interceptor drones have proven effective at shooting down Russia’s older piston-engine Geran-2 one-way attack drones.

In response, Russia is transitioning to the more expensive, but harder to intercept, jet-powered one-way attack drone, with production now rising to around 4,000 units monthly.

Key to the success of counter-drone solutions is cost and mass. While Helsing didn’t provide specifics, it said that “mass production” is to start at its Resilience Factories, and that unit prices will “significantly undercut” those of existing missile interceptors.

Helsing is already working with Ukraine on counter-drone and other defence technologies. It is also one of Europe’s leading companies developing advanced Collaborative Combat Aircraft through its CA-1 Europa programme.

]]> American Airlines has received its first Embraer E175 regional jet equipped with RECARO’s new-generation R2 passenger seats. It is the first US airline to introduce the seating on the aircraft type.

Embraer continues to update the E175 cabin to improve passenger comfort and maintain the aircraft’s competitiveness in the regional jet market.

The new seats will enter service on American Eagle flights this autumn, according to RECARO Aircraft Seating.

What is different about the new RECARO R2 seats?

The R2 is designed for short- and medium-haul flights, with a slimmer backrest that increases passengers’ knee clearance and personal space.

The seat also includes a six-way adjustable headrest and a tablet holder, letting passengers securely place their own devices for viewing entertainment during the flight.

American’s installation features customised seat covers and finishes matching the airline’s updated regional cabin design. In 2025, American announced plans to retrofit its regional fleet to a harmonised design standard, including all the CRJ700, CRJ900, E170 and E175 aircraft operated by its regional carriers. The RECARO seats installed on the E175 feature the new blue and amber design aesthetic.

RECARO said American selected the R2 partly because of its pre-certification qualifications and the manufacturer’s ability to meet the airline’s planned entry-into-service schedule.

“As the first US airline to introduce RECARO seats on Embraer E175 aircraft, we’re continuing to raise the bar for regional travel,” said Rhonda Crawford, senior vice president of customer experience design and strategy at American Airlines. “Our goal is to deliver the elevated experience customers want, while creating greater consistency across the American travel experience.”

Embraer continues upgrading its E175 regional jet

Embraer is investing in the first-generation E175, which is widely used by US regional airlines. The Brazilian planemaker said the cabin improvements bring the passenger experience closer to that offered by its newer E2 aircraft family.

“The introduction of our new RECARO seats demonstrates our commitment to investing in the platform and delivering enhancements that improve passenger experience while creating additional value for operators,” said Arjan Meijer, president and CEO of Embraer Commercial Aviation.

The manufacturer is also introducing technology to the E175, including enhanced data connectivity and next-generation weather radar, improving operational capability, situational awareness and efficiency.

The E175 remains an important aircraft for US regional operations. Its capacity and weight allow airlines to operate within scope clause pilot contract restrictions that limit the size of aircraft flown by regional partners.

RECARO expands its presence on Embraer aircraft

The American Airlines installation also marks another development in the relationship between Embraer and RECARO, which is entering its third year.

Mark Hiller, chief executive and shareholder of RECARO Aircraft Seating and CEO of RECARO Holding, said: “Seeing our R2 seat enter the US market on an Embraer E175 for the first time with American Airlines is a significant milestone for RECARO.”

The R2 is part of RECARO’s current seating portfolio, designed to combine passenger comfort with lightweight construction and durability for airline operations.

The first delivery establishes the new seating option on the E175 platform, giving airlines another cabin configuration option for the regional jet.
